exercises: A class studies water drying from a wet cloth. Identify two topics from this year’s book that connect to its question, and explain each connection.
Two paper planes are launched by different students from different heights. Their distances differ. Explain why this does not isolate the effect of the wingtips. Describe a fairer comparison.
A learner reports only the longest of three flights. What information has been lost? Explain why three flights cannot establish that a design always travels farther.
Someone suggests paving a school’s muddy patch. What evidence about water movement and the uses of the space would help judge the proposal? Name one safety precaution when gathering it.
glossary: An expected observation under stated conditions.
Information used to judge an idea or answer a question.
A comparison that keeps other relevant conditions alike while testing a particular difference.
Something accepted for the moment without having checked it.
The change of liquid water into water vapour at its surface.
The change of water vapour into liquid water.

lesson.text: 1.1  Ask Deeper Questions

Suppose you think that folding up a paper plane’s wingtips will change how far it travels. Your explanation is an idea to investigate. A **prediction** states what you expect to observe under particular conditions. Before launching, predict whether the folded tips will increase the distance, decrease it or make no clear difference.
lesson.addition: Turn the source’s flight invitation into a testable comparison.
One fair-comparison investigation with repeated trials and no prescribed result.
paragraphs: With your teacher, make two paper planes from identical sheets using the same basic folds. Label them A and B. Keep A’s wingtips flat; fold both of B’s wingtips upward by the same amount. Use only paper, without clips or pointed attachments.
1. Choose a clear indoor space. Mark a launch line. Use the same launcher, launch height and direction, and aim for the same gentle release each time.

2. Launch A, then B. Measure straight from the launch line to the point where each plane first touches the floor, in the intended forward direction. Record each distance and its unit in your notebook.
3. Alternate A and B until each has made three flights. Note turns, collisions or damaged folds; do not quietly replace an inconvenient result.
4. Compare all three distances for each plane. Describe any pattern and any overlap. What would you test again?
Keep everyone behind the launch line. Never aim at a person. Retrieve planes only when launching has stopped. Hand launches vary, so these trials cannot establish a rule for every plane.

lesson.text: A **fair comparison** keeps other relevant conditions alike while testing a particular difference. Here the intended difference is the wingtips. The paper, basic folds and launch conditions should stay alike. A record of only the longest flight would hide how much the other flights varied.
lesson.addition: Explain controls and why all trial records matter.
A substantial evidence pause after the first-hand comparison.
paragraphs: Suppose one plane travelled farther on its first flight, but the distances for the two planes overlapped across the three trials. Would “This design always flies farther” be a justified conclusion?

Discuss how differences in a hand launch, a bent wing or where a plane first lands could affect your record. Choose one detail to control more carefully on the next set of flights. Explain what more evidence would help you decide.

lesson.text: Your conclusion should describe what your records support. “B travelled farther in two of our three pairs of flights” is a narrower claim than “B is the better plane”. Better for what: distance, time in the air or a straight path? The question determines what you need to measure.
lesson.addition: Distinguish observed patterns from universal claims and define the comparison criterion.

lesson.text: Scientific explanations can change when new evidence becomes available. An unexpected result is a reason to examine the test, the record and the explanation. It is not a reason to hide the result. Even a result that agrees with your prediction may leave something unanswered.
1.2  Ideas Connect Across Science

This book brings together physics, chemistry, biology and earth science. Their questions overlap. A paper plane involves the properties of paper, forces, motion and measurement. Understanding rain brings together water, heat, air and the ground beneath our feet. The chapters ahead develop these connections.

items: Compare acidic, basic and neutral substances.
Investigate questions about sour fruits and a haldi stain.

Test which materials let a lamp glow in a circuit.

Connect a material’s properties with its uses.

Compare melting ice, ripening fruit and rocks breaking.
Ask which changes can be reversed, and how.

lesson.text: A battery running out is one example of change, but not all batteries are alike. Some are designed to be recharged; others are not. Never try to recharge a battery that is not designed for it. The label and correct equipment matter. “Used up” does not tell the whole story.
lesson.correction: Replace the source’s blanket claim that a depleted torch battery cannot be used again.

lesson.text: A spoon can form part of a test circuit’s path. If a lamp stays dark, check the cell, lamp and connections before drawing a conclusion about the object. A faulty connection can also interrupt the path.
lesson.addition: Retain the spoon test and bound a negative observation; the photo is a component close-up, not that exact test.

columns.title: Growing and changing
items: Explore adolescence as a stage of growth and change.
Recognise that people develop at different rates.
Discuss questions respectfully, without comparing classmates’ bodies.

columns.title: Heat in nature
items: Investigate how heat moves between places.
Connect heating and cooling with changes in water.
Follow links among sunlight, evaporation and rain.

lesson.caption: From a candle to sunlight: heating connects everyday changes with water in nature. Observe flames only in a teacher-led demonstration.
lesson.addition: Use real candle and lake photographs with the complete evaporation/condensation explanation adjacent.

lesson.text: Liquid water enters the air as water vapour during **evaporation**. When water vapour cools sufficiently, **condensation** forms tiny liquid droplets; clouds may contain droplets, ice crystals or both. Water can later fall as rain, flow over land or soak into the ground. Sunlight supplies energy for much of this cycling; water vapour itself is invisible.
lesson.correction: Make condensation explicit between evaporation and rain; do not represent visible cloud as vapour.

items: Investigate ways to measure time.
Relate a moving object’s distance to the time taken.
Compare measurements, rather than impressions such as “fast”.

Study breathing and how blood carries nutrients.
Connect these processes with growth and survival.

columns.title: Life processes in plants
items: Investigate how plants make food and exchange gases.
Explore how plants obtain water and other substances.
Compare plant and animal processes without assuming they work identically.

Investigate shadows and reflections.
Connect changing shadows with ways of tracking time.

lesson.caption: A pencil seen through water and glass. Keep light beams away from eyes.
lesson.addition: Use a real pencil-in-water photograph to preview the source light-and-water connection; retain eye safety.

lesson.text: The final chapter turns to Earth, the Moon and the Sun. Earth rotates about its axis and travels around the Sun; the Moon travels around Earth. These movements help explain day and night and the changing positions we observe. Earth and the Moon can also cast shadows that produce eclipses. Never look directly at the Sun to investigate these ideas.

lesson.caption: Sunlight illuminates one half of Earth. During a solar eclipse, the Moon lies between the Sun and Earth and its shadow falls on part of Earth. These photographs show separate views.
lesson.addition: Use real Galileo and National Park Service photographs as separate observations, not an alignment diagram.

lesson.text: Plant and animal life processes developed through evolution over many generations. Organisms did not plan these changes. Compare their shared needs and different structures without assuming they work identically.
lesson.correction: Replace purposeful “life figured out how” wording with a non-teleological explanation.

lesson.text: 1.3  Explore with Care

Investigating the world also brings responsibility. Human activities affect water, soil, air and living things. Scientific evidence can help people understand environmental problems and judge proposed solutions. A useful suggestion needs a reason for expecting it to help, and a way to check what happens.

For example, rainwater may soak into open ground or flow across a paved surface. If a school wants to reduce puddling, it needs to understand where the water comes from and where it goes. One photograph after one shower cannot show how the site behaves in every storm.
lesson.addition: Use the source’s groundwater link to illustrate responsible evidence gathering.

lesson.text: Compare records after different showers from a safe, dry place; consider slope, surface and drainage. Never enter floodwater or open drains. Discuss changes with responsible adults, considering evidence, safety, cost and how people use the space.
lesson.addition: Give environmental responsibility a concrete evidence-based application without adding a second investigation.

lesson.text: Share your question, method and evidence. If others disagree, discuss which observation could help resolve it. Ask for guidance when you need unfamiliar equipment.
1.4  Question the Answer

Usually you are given a question and asked for an answer. Try reversing the task. A single answer may fit very different questions. “Just make it half!” could respond to sharing a cake equally, shortening an essay, fitting something into an envelope or reducing the length of a dance song.

paragraphs: For each answer below, invent an interesting question or situation that could lead to it. Write your questions in your notebook, then compare them with a partner.
• Because the cat’s teeth were crooked.
• Just add some milk.
• Don’t panic, I have my towel.
Try different contexts, rather than an obvious arithmetic question for 42. Which facts would need to be true for each answer to fit? Identify an assumption in one of your situations.

lesson.text: This is an exercise in creative question-making. An imagined situation is not scientific evidence, and an answer can contain an assumption that turns out to be mistaken. Choose one of your questions and discuss whether observation could help answer it. If not, explain what kind of question it is.
lesson.correction: Retain the creative task without treating every premise as true or every question as scientifically testable.

lesson.text: A question about a story may invite imaginative answers. A question about a material needs observations that other people can check. State which kind of question you are asking, and which information your answer depends on.
lesson.addition: Link the restored experiment-preview pictures with the limits of creative question-making.

lesson.text: Keep room for questions that you cannot answer yet. New knowledge, a better measurement or a different comparison may let you return to them. The next chapters offer places to begin: look closely, test carefully and let the evidence help you rethink.

opener: Watch a paper plane. What would you like to find out about its flight?

Perhaps it turns, dips or travels farther than you expected. One flight may raise several questions: What changed its direction? Would it follow the same path again? What could you measure instead of guessing?

In Class 6, you began observing, questioning and testing ideas. In Class 7, you will look more closely at how things work, why changes happen and what patterns can tell you. Curiosity still starts the journey; careful evidence helps you decide where to go next.

Science reaches from tiny cells in a leaf to the movement of Earth and the Moon. It also begins with things near you: a stain on cloth, a lamp that will not light or water soaking into the ground. Familiar things can lead to unfamiliar questions.
summary: Science develops through questions, observations, tests and explanations that can change with evidence.
A clear question tells you what to observe or measure. A prediction states what you expect before a test.
Fair comparisons and repeated trials help you interpret results, including those you did not expect.
Materials, energy, motion, life processes and Earth’s systems are connected topics.
Responsible investigation considers the environment, other people and safe ways of working.
Creative questions can open new directions. Check their assumptions before treating an answer as an explanation.

Three containers tested with the same red rose extract give these colours: A green, B unchanged purple, C red-pink. Suggest the nature of each. For which container would another indicator be especially useful, and why?

Manya cannot use a visual colour change in a teacher-led demonstration. Which kind of indicator might provide a smell-based comparison using approved samples? Explain its limits and precautions. Do not blindfold anyone or test unknown chemicals.

Suggest two possible pairs of writing liquid and revealing indicator for a hidden message. In your notebook, make a table naming each pair and the predicted colour. Explain how you would test the prediction safely.
Grape juice turns red rose extract reddish. Baking soda solution is added gradually. What changes might occur if enough is added? Explain why the starting amounts and concentrations matter.
Keerthi writes with orange juice and lets it dry. Suggest an indicator that could help reveal the acidic writing. Why would turmeric alone be a poor choice? Describe a control patch.

Liquid X turns red rose extract green. What is its likely nature? Predict what sufficient excess amla juice might do to the colour, and explain your reasoning.

Reconstruct this decision map in your notebook: poor plant growth → test soil → compare the result with the crop’s needs → choose a response. Name a suitable indicator or soil test; describe responses for overly acidic and overly basic soil. Add a branch for soil near the required range.

A solution nature that can turn red litmus blue; also called alkaline.
Neither acidic nor basic; not a synonym for safe.

The liquid that passes through a filter.

lesson.text: 2.1  Nature as a Science Laboratory

A liquid can look colourless without being water. Colour, smell and familiarity do not tell us whether it is safe. In this chapter, use only small amounts of samples selected and diluted by your teacher. Wear eye protection, protect the work surface and wash your hands afterwards. Never taste a test sample or touch it to identify its nature.
lesson.correction: Replace tasting and rubbing samples with safe observations and recalled food experience.

lesson.text: Compare both colours of litmus

Blue and red litmus papers let us compare a sample in two ways. Before testing, look at unused pieces of both papers. Will every liquid affect them in the same way? Record what happens before assigning the samples to a group.

lesson.figureCaption: Start with unused red and blue papers. Use a fresh piece for each drop.
paragraphs: Test teacher-prepared lemon juice, soap solution, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar, baking soda solution, lime water, tap water, washing powder solution, sugar solution and salt solution. Include one other sample only with approval.
1. Place separate small pieces of blue and red litmus on a clean, dry white tile. Label the positions so you can identify each sample.
2. Put one drop of a sample on one blue piece and one red piece. Use separate droppers, or clean and rinse the dropper between samples.
3. Compare each piece with unused paper. Record both final colours in your notebook. Repeat for every sample; record unclear changes as unclear.
Keep samples away from eyes and mouths. Your teacher handles lime water and washing powder solution. Do not test cleaners, bleach or unknown liquids from home.

lesson.caption: Table 2.1  Record observations before classifying
lesson.note: Notebook record guide, not a table of results. Read across to pair the two observations for one sample; compare down to find patterns.

lesson.text: **Lime water** is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water. It is not juice from the lime fruit. A teacher can prepare it using suitable laboratory materials and separate the clear liquid from undissolved solid. Do not mix quicklime with water yourself: the process releases considerable heat and can splash an irritating mixture.
lesson.correction: Retain the chemical identity; replace student quicklime preparation with a teacher-only preparation note.

items: Group A: blue paper turns red; red paper remains red.
Group B: red paper turns blue; blue paper remains blue.
Group C: neither paper shows a clear change.

lesson.text: Make three lists headed A, B and C in your notebook, using the three observed patterns. Put each sample in the list supported by both tests. Keep doubtful results separate for retesting rather than forcing them into a group.
lesson.addition: Bound uncertain observations and avoid pre-filled student results.

lesson.text: Suppose two groups test the same soap solution and report different colours. Check whether the papers began with the same colour, whether a dropper carried over another sample and whether the paper was wet already. Test fresh pieces using the same solution. Keep the first observations in the record as well as the repeat; crossing out an inconvenient result would hide the reason for checking it.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to sort-record

lesson.text: From observations to names

An **acid-base indicator** changes colour in response to the acidic or basic nature of a solution. Litmus is made from dyes obtained from certain lichens and is supplied as a solution or as paper strips. Some other indicators come from plants; synthetic indicators are manufactured. The indicator supplies evidence through its response; the original colour of the sample alone is not the test.

columns.title: Acidic
items: Evidence: blue litmus turns red.
Typical samples: lemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water and vinegar.
Classroom group: A.

columns.title: Basic
items: Evidence: red litmus turns blue.
Typical samples: soap, baking soda, lime water and washing powder solutions.
Classroom group: B.

columns.title: Neutral
items: Meaning: neither acidic nor basic.
Typical reference samples: pure water and suitable sugar or common salt solutions in pure water.
Classroom group: C, if neither paper changes; this is a limited test.

lesson.text: Litmus does not measure an exact value of acidity. A very weak change can be hard to see, and a coloured sample can mask it. Tap water varies from place to place. “No clear change in either paper” is your observation; it does not prove that every water sample is exactly neutral or safe to drink.
lesson.correction: Qualify the source classification of tap water and distinguish observations from exact neutrality.

lesson.text: Consider two samples that leave blue litmus blue. One could be basic; another could be neutral. Blue paper alone has not separated them. Red paper adds a second comparison: a basic sample can turn it blue, while a neutral reference leaves it red. This is why a test that produces no visible change can still be informative when it is combined with another observation.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to neutral-limit

lesson.heading: A living source of colour
lesson.text: A lichen is a close association involving a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually an alga or a cyanobacterium. Look for lichens on bark or rocks without removing them. Different lichens tolerate different conditions, so finding one is not a complete test of air quality.
lesson.caption: Lichen growing on a small piece of bark.
lesson.correction: Extend the alga-only definition and avoid treating all lichens as proof of clean air.

lesson.text: Familiar foods, careful comparisons

paragraphs: Recall the taste of lemon, curd or tamarind that you have eaten as food. What do these familiar foods have in common? Do not taste the samples prepared for an investigation.

Some bases feel slippery and many taste bitter, but these are unsafe identification tests. Bitter gourd tastes bitter without being classified as a base. Explain why “bitter” is not enough evidence for “basic”.
Use a reference source to identify acids commonly present in lemon, curd, tamarind and vinegar. Compare your findings with the table below. A food can contain more than one acid.

lesson.caption: Table 2.2  Acids in familiar foods
rows: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and citric acid
lesson.note: Reference examples, not permission to taste laboratory samples. These names do not imply that a food contains only one acid.

lesson.text: An acid named in a food is one ingredient among many. A lemon is not a container of pure citric acid, and different fruits contain different amounts. Dilution changes how much acid is present in each drop. Do not rank foods by sourness in this investigation, or assume that an edible food makes every concentrated chemical with the same acid name safe to handle.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to food-table

lesson.text: Make an indicator from red roses

Can a flower supply a useful indicator? A coloured liquid obtained from a plant is an **extract**. Preparing the extract and testing it are separate tasks: first collect the colour, then compare its behaviour in known samples. Water carries some of the petal pigments into the liquid. Filtering removes petal pieces, which would otherwise make it harder to compare colours through the glass.

lesson.figureCaption: Washed petals, a mortar and a filtered extract. Let hot equipment cool.
paragraphs: 1. Collect a handful of fallen red rose petals, without plucking flowers. Use clean, suitable petals selected by your teacher; wash them with water.
2. Crush the petals with a mortar and pestle. Put them in a heat-resistant container.
3. Ask an adult to add enough hot water to cover the petals. Cover the container and wait 5–10 minutes. Let it cool before handling.
4. Filter the liquid into a clean container. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate. Keep some untreated extract for comparison.
Only an adult handles hot water. Label the extract; it is for testing, not drinking.

lesson.text: Describe the colour of the fresh extract before testing it. Petal variety, freshness and the amount of water can affect its appearance. An extract that is very pale or cloudy may give an unclear result. Checking it with known samples helps you decide whether it is useful.
lesson.addition: Explain preparation variability and a reference control.

lesson.text: During filtration, the paper holds back larger pieces while the coloured liquid passes through. The colour does not have to disappear for filtration to work: dissolved pigment can remain in the filtrate. Compare the filtered extract with the liquid containing petals. Which one gives a clearer view of a later colour change? This separates removing solid pieces from removing every substance in the liquid.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to extract-check

paragraphs: 1. Put the same amount of cooled red rose extract, about 10–20 drops, into three small transparent containers. Label them A, B and control.
2. Add about 20–30 drops of lemon juice to A and the same number of drops of soap solution to B. Keep the control unchanged. Use clean droppers.
3. Compare all three against white paper in the same light. Record the sample, the observed colour and the nature suggested by your earlier litmus test.
4. Test the remaining approved samples in fresh portions of extract. Keep the extract amount and sample amount alike across comparisons.
Do the samples that affected blue litmus show a similar rose-extract colour? What about samples that affected red litmus? Record disagreement rather than changing a result to match your prediction.

lesson.caption: Table 2.3  Read the rose test alongside the litmus test
rows: What you saw; compare with control
lesson.note: This is a recording guide. Compare down only after completing your own observations.

lesson.text: Imagine that a very dark fruit juice makes the mixture look red before the indicator has a clear effect. A red appearance alone would not show which material supplied that colour. Look at a small portion of the sample without indicator as well as the untreated extract. A separate litmus test provides another line of evidence. If the colour remains hard to interpret, record that limit instead of assigning a confident label.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to rose-guide

lesson.text: A suitable red rose extract commonly becomes a shade of red or pink in an acidic sample and green in a basic sample. A sample that gives little change needs comparison with the untreated extract and the litmus tests. The exact shade depends on the extract and sample: a printed colour is a guide, not a measurement.

lesson.caption: Illustrative comparison after testing: green, unchanged purple and red-pink. These are reference colours, not a record of your experiment.

lesson.text: Red hibiscus (gudhal), purple cabbage, jamun, beetroot and turmeric provide other colours to investigate. Do not assume that every coloured extract distinguishes acids and bases equally well. Compare each candidate with known acidic and basic samples and an untreated control.
lesson.correction: Present candidate plant pigments as indicators to validate, not equally reliable universal tests.

lesson.heading: Flower colour has more than one cause
lesson.text: Some hydrangeas produce blue flowers when acidic soil makes aluminium available to the plant. The same kinds may produce pink flowers when less aluminium is available. Variety matters too; white flowers do not simply turn blue. Soil conditions can affect colour, but a flower is not a substitute for a soil test.
lesson.caption: Blue and pink hydrangea flower heads.
lesson.correction: Add aluminium availability and cultivar limits to the source soil-colour claim.

lesson.text: A colour change inside a plant and a colour change in a test tube are related questions, but they are not identical tests. Roots take up substances, and flowers develop over time. Changing garden soil today will not instantly recolour every flower. To compare two plants fairly, consider their variety, growing conditions and the time of observation as well as the soil result.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to hydrangea

lesson.text: What can turmeric tell us?

Turmeric, or haldi, is a yellow spice from a plant in the ginger family. Its colour can be carried on paper. Unlike a two-colour litmus test, this indicator has a useful limitation: two different kinds of sample can give the same visible result. Keep a reference strip untreated so that drying, lighting or the original shade of the paper is not mistaken for a reaction to a sample.

lesson.figureCaption: Turmeric paste and unused yellow paper strips, ready for testing.
paragraphs: 1. Mix a spoonful of turmeric with a little water to make a paste. Fresh turmeric may be ground instead, with adult help.
2. Dip filter paper in the paste until it becomes yellow. Lift it out and let it dry. With adult supervision, cut it into strips.
3. Place a drop of each approved sample on a separate strip. Leave an unused strip beside them for comparison.
4. In your notebook, record the sample name and the final colour of its strip. Group samples with a similar result, then compare with your litmus groups.
Keep the paste and samples away from eyes and mouths. Use scissors carefully. Do not treat a missing colour change as a failed experiment; it may be evidence about the test.

lesson.text: Turmeric paper usually turns reddish-brown with a basic solution. It stays yellow with acidic and neutral solutions. It can therefore help identify a base, but an unchanged yellow strip cannot distinguish an acid from a neutral solution. Use both litmus papers to make that comparison.

paragraphs: Two samples leave turmeric paper yellow. One is vinegar and one is sugar solution. Can you decide which is which from that observation alone?
Choose another test and predict the two possible results. Explain why repeating only the turmeric test, even very carefully, would not supply the missing distinction.

lesson.text: An unchanged strip is useful only if the indicator is working. Use a small known basic reference chosen by your teacher to check a fresh piece of turmeric paper. If that reference also gives no clear change, investigate the paper or preparation before judging the unknown sample. A control does not provide the unknown answer; it checks whether the test can produce the response you are looking for.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to turmeric-think

lesson.text: A yellow curry stain may become reddish-brown when soap reaches it because the soap solution is basic. This links an everyday observation with the indicator test. Turmeric also has a long history of culinary and traditional use. Such use does not by itself establish that a preparation treats a disease; health claims need appropriate evidence.
lesson.correction: Retain the cultural context without asserting unproven health benefits.

lesson.text: Ashwin makes a greeting card for his teacher at Guru Purnima, writing in Odia. He coats paper with turmeric, lets it dry and uses a teacher-approved soap solution to write a message. Explain the colour he might see. Respect for a teacher can be expressed in any language; the chemistry of the indicator does not depend on the words.
An indicator detected by smell

Some substances show a change in detectable smell in acidic or basic conditions. They are called **olfactory indicators**. Smell is a less precise observation than it may seem: people differ in sensitivity, and repeatedly smelling the same substance can make it harder to notice. The sample’s own smell can also mask another smell. A control and a second kind of indicator help you avoid treating an uncertain impression as a definite identification.
lesson.addition: Bound the reliability of smell observations.

lesson.figureCaption: An onion container and three separate cotton strips. Keep a control strip.
paragraphs: This is a teacher-led demonstration using only approved food-based samples. Nobody is blindfolded. Do not participate in smelling if onion triggers discomfort or an allergy.
1. An adult chops onion and puts it with clean cotton or filter-paper strips in a closed container overnight.
2. Place three strips on separate clean surfaces. Keep one unchanged. Add a few drops of tamarind water to one and baking soda solution to another.
3. Only if your teacher approves, compare the smells by gently wafting air from a distance; never put a sample near your nose or inhale directly.
4. Record the smell before and after, including “no clear difference”. Compare with the unchanged strip. The teacher may repeat with other approved dilute samples.
Does your record distinguish the samples? If not, use a colour indicator. Never smell unknown laboratory chemicals or cleaning products.

lesson.text: The detectable onion smell may be reduced in basic conditions while remaining noticeable in acidic conditions. Results can be subtle with dilute baking soda. A weak smell, an unsuitable concentration or differences between observers can make the test inconclusive. It is not a way to identify arbitrary unknown liquids safely.
lesson.correction: Avoid promising a guaranteed smell result with dilute baking soda.

lesson.text: Suppose one observer notices less onion smell and another reports no difference. Record both descriptions. The amount of onion on each strip, the time allowed for the drops to spread and each person’s sensitivity may affect the comparison. Repeatedly taking a stronger sniff is not the solution. Discuss the uncertainty, then choose a safe colour test if the class needs clearer evidence.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to onion-explain

lesson.text: 2.2  When Acids and Bases Meet

An indicator reports the state of a mixture at the time you test it. If you add an acidic solution to a basic one, will the indicator keep its original colour? A drop-by-drop comparison helps you watch the change without assuming that equal volumes must balance each other. A concentrated solution contains more dissolved substance in a given volume than a dilute one. Similar-looking drops can therefore supply different amounts of the substances that react.

lesson.figureCaption: Teacher demonstration: a small test tube, dropper and clear solutions before mixing.
paragraphs: Your teacher performs this demonstration with eye protection, dilute prepared lime water and a stable test-tube rack. Do not prepare quicklime or mix household cleaners.
1. Put one drop of lemon juice and about twenty drops of water in a test tube. Observe its appearance; add a drop of blue litmus solution.
2. Record the colour. Add lime water one drop at a time, gently swirling after each drop. Record the sequence of colours and approximate drop count.
3. If the mixture becomes blue, stop adding lime water. Predict what adding lemon juice might do. Add one drop, mix and observe; if needed, continue a drop at a time.
Does one drop always reverse the colour? Compare your prediction with the record. The teacher disposes of the mixtures as directed for the materials used.

lesson.text: In **neutralisation**, an acid reacts with a base. For the acid and hydroxide base used here, the reaction forms a salt and water and releases heat. The amount used in this demonstration may be too small to make a temperature change easy to notice. A colour change alone does not measure heat.
lesson.correction: Bound acid-plus-base equation to the hydroxide case; no claim of perceptible warming in this tiny demonstration.

lesson.text: Acid + hydroxide base → salt + water
lesson.caption: Heat is released in this neutralisation. “Salt” names a family of substances, not only the common salt used in food.

lesson.text: Adding lime water reduces the acidic effect of the lemon juice. Enough added base can leave the mixture basic: blue litmus solution at the end is evidence of excess base, not proof of neutrality. Adding enough acid can make the mixture acidic again. The outcome depends on how much acid and base react, not just on equal numbers of drops.
lesson.correction: Correct the source equation of a blue endpoint with a neutral solution.

lesson.text: Think of each added drop as supplying another small amount of reactant. Early drops of base may react while acid is still left. Later drops may supply more base than the remaining acid can react with. Stirring matters because an unmixed drop can briefly create a local colour different from the rest of the liquid. Judge the well-mixed sample, and record the sequence rather than only its final colour.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to endpoint

paragraphs: One group says, “We mixed an acid with a base, so the result must be neutral.” Another says, “Our mixture turned blue, so some base is left.” Which statement uses the observation more carefully?
Explain why adding one drop of lemon juice might fail to reverse the colour. What information about the amounts and concentrations would help you predict the next change?

lesson.text: Prafulla Chandra Ray: research and education

Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861–1944) was a chemist, teacher and industrial pioneer, often called the Father of Modern Indian Chemistry. After doctoral study in Britain, he returned to India and helped develop chemical research and teaching. His Bengal Chemical enterprise became a limited company in 1901. He also wrote about the history of chemistry in India and supported education through Indian languages.
lesson.correction: Use the company incorporation date precisely; omit unnecessary absolute first-company wording.

lesson.text: 2.3  Chemistry in Daily Life

A farmer notices poor growth. Is the soil too acidic, too basic, short of nutrients, too wet or affected by something else? Plant appearance alone does not identify the cause. Some fertilisers can make soil more acidic over time, but a soil test and knowledge of the crop should guide treatment.

lesson.caption: Compare a soil sample with a tested reference. Poor growth needs investigation before treatment.

columns.title: Soil too acidic for the crop
items: Evidence: a suitable soil test shows excessive acidity for that crop.
Response: an expert may recommend a measured amount of agricultural lime.
Check: retest later; adding too much can create another problem.

columns.title: Soil too basic for the crop
items: Evidence: a soil test and crop needs identify the problem.
Response: seek local agricultural advice; suitable organic matter may help soil condition.
Check: compost is not a guaranteed or rapid cure for alkaline soil.

columns.title: Soil near the required range
items: Evidence: acidity alone does not explain the poor growth.
Response: investigate nutrients, drainage, watering, pests and other conditions.
Check: choose a treatment for the cause supported by evidence.

lesson.text: An ant bite is sometimes described as an acid-base problem. Some ants use formic acid in defence, but bites and stings differ between species. Skin reactions are not simply a beaker experiment. Tell an adult after a bite; wash the area with soap and water and use a wrapped cold compress. Do not apply test chemicals or baking-soda remedies. Seek urgent help for breathing difficulty or swelling of the mouth or throat.
lesson.correction: Replace blanket acid-neutralisation first aid with current NHS guidance; retain the example as a limit of the model.

lesson.text: Gurbir notices fewer fish in a lake near factories. Acidic waste is one possible cause, not a conclusion from the fish count alone. Oxygen shortage, toxic substances, temperature and other changes also matter. Treatment plants may adjust the acidity of wastewater before discharge, but a neutral reading does not prove the water is free of harmful substances. Treatment and testing belong with trained people, before waste enters the lake.
lesson.correction: Neutralisation is one treatment step, not proof of safe industrial discharge.

lesson.text: To investigate the lake responsibly, trained people would compare samples from suitable locations and times, including water away from the suspected discharge. Records before and after treatment would be more useful than one photograph. Students can discuss such evidence without collecting polluted water. Separating a possible explanation from a demonstrated cause is part of deciding what action could actually protect the fish.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to waste

lesson.text: Return to the hidden message

One explanation for the science-fair message is that a basic soap solution was used to write on the paper and allowed to dry. Wetting it with turmeric indicator would make the writing reddish-brown against yellow paper. Other indicator-and-solution pairs are possible. Suggest a prediction that would distinguish two explanations, rather than claiming that a colourful result proves one recipe.

Compare a patch written with soap solution with a patch wetted only with water. Let both dry, then apply the same indicator in the same way. If only the soap patch develops the predicted colour, the comparison supports the role of the writing liquid. If both patches change alike, examine the paper and indicator before claiming that the message has been explained.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to fair-explain

lesson.text: For a teacher-approved demonstration, test a tiny patch first and brush indicator onto paper instead of spraying it towards people. Use small quantities and keep food for eating separate from test materials. A visible message connects art and chemistry; a careful comparison explains why it appears.
lesson.addition: Use brush application to avoid aerosols; preserve the creative natural-indicator connection.

opener: A blank sheet. A few drops. A hidden message appears. What changed?

At a school science fair on National Science Day, 28 February, Ashwin and Keerthi receive sheets that seem to be blank. A volunteer wets the paper with a liquid, and a welcome message becomes visible. The children wonder whether the paper, the writing or the liquid explains the change.

At another stall, familiar substances produce different colours when mixed with plant extracts. These observations offer a way to investigate the mystery. You will compare substances, prepare indicators and use evidence to decide what a colour change can tell you.
Keep the message in mind as you work. By the end of the chapter, you will be able to suggest a possible explanation and a safe way to check it.

projects.title: A different reaction
projects.text: Vinegar produces bubbles with eggshell or marble, while soap solution produces no clear bubbling. Both solids contain calcium carbonate. With your teacher, explain how an acid reacting with a carbonate can release carbon dioxide. Why is this not the same observable result as the lime-water neutralisation? Never seal a gas-producing mixture in a container.

projects.title: Colour, pattern and prediction
projects.text: Plan a small indicator rangoli on scrap paper using approved mild substances. Predict colours before applying drops or using a brush. Keep a record of each mixture, minimise waste and protect skin, eyes and surfaces. Compare the finished colours with your predictions.

projects.title: Compare local water safely
projects.text: With adult help, obtain safe samples of rainwater and tap water. A teacher may supply other samples; do not enter a river or collect polluted water. Compare them using indicators and a reference sample. Explain why the test cannot establish whether the water is drinkable.

projects.title: Investigate a local soil
projects.text: With permission, take a small soil sample without disturbing roots. Ask your teacher to prepare a water extract or use a suitable soil-testing kit. Record where it came from, the method and the result. Compare with the needs of a chosen plant; do not add treatments merely to change a colour. If comparing two sites, explain how you would keep the amounts of soil and water alike.

summary: Use indicators and evidence to compare acidic, basic and neutral solutions. Never taste or touch test samples to identify them.
Acidic samples turn blue litmus red; basic samples turn red litmus blue. Use both papers and record unclear results.
Litmus comes from certain lichens. Plant extracts can also provide indicators, but their performance needs checking.
A suitable red rose extract commonly becomes red-pink in acidic samples and green in basic ones; compare with an untreated control.
Turmeric turns reddish-brown with a base. Remaining yellow does not distinguish an acidic sample from a neutral one.
Olfactory indicators involve a change in detectable smell. They require safe materials and may give inconclusive observations.
Neutralisation of an acid by a hydroxide base forms a salt and water and releases heat. An excess of either reactant can remain.
Soil and wastewater treatment require tests and suitable expertise. A neutral result does not mean a sample is safe.
A hidden-message demonstration uses a difference in indicator colour. Several recipes may explain the same visible result.

Draw a circuit diagram for a simple incandescent torch. Include the cell or battery, lamp, connecting wires and switch. Show its ON and OFF states.

glossary: A source that supplies electrical energy through chemical changes.
A connection point on a cell or component.
An arrangement of components and connections that can provide a path for current.
The fine wire heated to glowing in an incandescent lamp.
A light-emitting diode, used with correct polarity and current limiting.
A device that completes or breaks a conducting path.
A component that resists current; here it limits current through an LED.
A material that allows current to flow relatively easily.
A material that strongly resists current under the conditions considered.

lesson.text: Electricity around us

Look around your home, school and neighbourhood without opening electrical equipment. Nihal’s group organised its examples by purpose. Add examples in your notebook, then propose a different grouping. A computer might fit more than one category: explain the purpose you have in mind.

items: Cooking: electric kettles, mixer grinders, toasters, ovens and microwave ovens.
Lighting: lamps in homes, offices, streets, markets and factories.
Transport and lifting: electric trains, buses, cars, scooters, lifts and escalators.
Heating and cooling: fans, room heaters, immersion heaters, geysers, refrigerators and air conditioners.
Entertainment and communication: televisions, radios, mobile phones and equipment that carries internet signals.
Other work: water pumps, cranes and computers used in schools, hospitals and workplaces.

lesson.text: Electrical energy can be supplied using moving water, wind, sunlight, or fuels such as coal and natural gas. Much of the electricity used in buildings arrives through a network of wires. A cell provides a portable source. The same word “electricity” does not make every source equally safe to investigate.

A kettle transfers electrical energy mainly into heating water. A fan transfers some into motion of its blades and the surrounding air. A lamp transfers some into light and some into heating. These examples suggest another grouping: what change does each device produce? One appliance can produce several changes, so explain your grouping instead of treating every category as exclusive.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting supply

lesson.text: Use only teacher-approved 1.5 V cells and holders for these activities. Never experiment with wall sockets, household wiring, generators, vehicle batteries or phone battery packs. Keep hands and the work area dry. Do not use leaking, swollen or damaged cells. Never join a cell’s two terminals directly with wire: a short circuit can make the cell and wire hot. Disconnect every circuit after a brief test.

The small cell in a torch lets us study connections without approaching the power network. Even then, a conducting object across its terminals can create a path that bypasses the lamp. That is different from an open circuit: an open path interrupts current, while a short path can allow too much. Keep spare wires and metal objects away from cell terminals.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting safe

lesson.text: 3.1  Inside a Torch

lesson.figureCaption: A battery torch, removable cap and cells. Inspect only the compartment intended to be opened.
paragraphs: 1. Take a small battery torch approved by your teacher. Locate its lamp and switch. Predict what moving the switch will do.
2. Move the switch to each position and record what the lamp does. If it does not light, record that too; do not assume the switch is the only possible cause.
3. Switch it off. With your teacher, open only its removable cell compartment. Note the number, direction and markings of the cells before removing them.
4. Draw the parts you can identify in your notebook. Do not force open a sealed or rechargeable torch.

lesson.text: A working torch commonly lights in one switch position and stays dark in the other. Inside are a source, a lamp and conducting connections. The switch changes a connection. To explain why that matters, we need to examine the parts and then trace the complete path through them.

A sketch is a record of what you can see, not a reason to invent hidden parts. Mark any connection you cannot inspect as uncertain. When you remove and replace cells, notice both the metal contacts and the direction of the cells. If a torch begins working afterwards, that observation alone cannot tell you whether you corrected the direction or improved a contact.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting torch-explain

lesson.text: The switch can move while the lamp stays dark. This suggests two different questions: did the switch change its own contact, and is the rest of the path working? As you study the separate components, keep these questions in mind. A working device depends on the parts cooperating, not simply on every part being present.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting torch-evidence

lesson.text: 3.2  A Simple Electrical Circuit
Cells and their terminals

paragraphs: 1. Inspect an undamaged cylindrical 1.5 V cell supplied by your teacher. Find its + and − markings. Compare the two ends without joining them.
2. Sketch the cell and label the marked ends. Describe the raised metal cap and the flatter metal end. Check your labels against the markings.
3. Look at an empty cell holder. Find its spring contacts and polarity marks. Predict how the cell should fit; ask your teacher to check before inserting it.

lesson.text: An **electric cell** is a source of electrical energy supplied by chemical changes inside it. Its two connection points are **terminals**: positive (+) and negative (−). On the familiar cylindrical cell, the raised metal cap is positive and the flat metal end is negative. Other cell shapes differ, so read the markings rather than relying on shape alone.

The number 1.5 V on a familiar cell is its stated voltage. Voltage describes the energy transferred per amount of charge; here it helps us choose a suitable source and lamp. It is not a count of how much charge remains in a used cell. Two cells with the same printed rating can behave differently if one is depleted or makes poor contact.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting cell-meaning

lesson.caption: A two-cell holder and loose cells. Follow the holder’s polarity marks; never force a cell into place.

lesson.text: Connecting cells together

paragraphs: 1. Use an approved two-cell torch with matching cells. With the switch off, record the original arrangement, then confirm that it works.
2. Switch off and swap the positions of the two cells while keeping each cell’s marked direction correct. Test briefly and record the result.
3. For comparison, draw what would happen if one cell were reversed. Your teacher may demonstrate this briefly in a suitable simple holder; do not reverse cells in electronic devices.
4. Restore the correct arrangement. Compare position with direction: are they the same thing?

lesson.text: In a **series** arrangement, the positive terminal of one cell joins the negative terminal of the next. With two matching 1.5 V cells correctly connected, their voltages add to about 3 V. Their metal links may be hidden inside a holder, even when the cells sit side by side. Follow the connections, not the shape of the case. In everyday use, “battery” can mean one cell or several cells connected together.

In the simple holder, swapping two matching working cells without changing their directions should leave the arrangement equivalent. Reversing one is different: their voltages oppose rather than add. A weak or absent light would be consistent with that change, but it would not by itself exclude a poor contact. Restore the original working arrangement to check the comparison.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting battery-explain

lesson.caption: Connections, not physical position, determine the series arrangement. The two free terminals supply the circuit.

lesson.text: More cells do not automatically make a device run longer. The arrangement changes the supply, and the device must be designed for it. Too high a voltage can damage a lamp or LED. Use the specified number and type of cells; do not mix old and new cells or try to recharge a non-rechargeable cell.
lesson.correction: Replace unconditional more-energy/longer-runtime claim with arrangement and device-rating qualifications.

lesson.text: A holder is more than a box that keeps cells tidy. Its springs and metal strips make electrical connections. With the cells removed, follow a visible strip from one contact to another and compare that route with the series diagram. If a link is hidden, consult the holder’s markings or your teacher instead of guessing. Do not bend the springs or insert metal tools to reach concealed contacts.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting battery-limit

lesson.text: Two ways to produce light

paragraphs: 1. Your teacher supplies a small incandescent torch lamp with an intact glass bulb. Observe its inside with a magnifier. Sketch the fine wire and its supports.
2. In a working torch or correctly rated holder, watch which part gives light during a brief test. Do not touch the lamp while it is on.
3. Disconnect the source and let the lamp cool. With help, inspect the metal case, separate centre tip and insulating material between them. Never break the glass.

lesson.text: The thin wire is the **filament**. Current through it transfers energy that heats it until it glows. Two support wires connect its ends to separate terminals: the metal case and the centre tip. Insulating material keeps those terminals apart. A connection to the glass does not connect to the filament.

Follow the internal route: one terminal connects to a support wire, then to the filament, then through the other support to the other terminal. The insulating part at the base prevents a direct metal bridge between the terminals. Current must pass through the filament for it to heat. This is why touching two wires to the same terminal does not substitute for using both terminals.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting lamp-meaning

paragraphs: 1. Observe an unconnected, new two-lead LED. Compare it with the incandescent lamp. Can you see a filament? Are the leads the same length?
2. Sketch the dome and both leads. Look for a flat edge on the casing. Your teacher checks the part’s information to confirm its terminal identification.
3. Do not connect the LED directly to cells. It needs a suitable current-limiting component as well as the correct connection direction.

lesson.caption: Left to right: incandescent torch lamp, LED and resistor. These enlarged component views are not to the same scale.

lesson.text: An **LED**, or light-emitting diode, produces light without a heated filament. On many new two-lead LEDs, the longer lead is the anode and the shorter lead is the cathode. The flat side commonly marks the cathode. Leads may have been cut, and some packages are different, so check the component information. A torch may contain several LEDs and additional electronics.

Look closely at the two devices before connecting them. The metal supports visible inside an LED package are not a glowing filament. A coloured plastic dome also does not mean that the LED is switched on. Record the unlit appearance first, then compare it with an approved working circuit. Distinguishing the material’s colour from emitted light avoids a misleading observation.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting led-meaning

columns.title: Incandescent lamp
items: Light-producing part: a heated filament.
Connections: two separate terminals leading to the filament.
Direction: normally lights with either cell polarity when correctly rated.

columns.title: LED
items: Light-producing part: a semiconductor, without a filament.
Connections: anode and cathode; check their identification.
Direction: normally lights in the forward direction, with current limited.

lesson.text: A torch lamp and an LED can both turn electrical energy into light, but they are not interchangeable in every holder. Their connections and supply requirements differ. Read the component rating with your teacher before substituting one for another. A component that does not light on a particular supply may still work on an appropriate supply; failure in one setup is not enough to call it broken.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting lamp-comparison

lesson.text: Both devices transfer energy, but the visible light is only part of the story. An incandescent filament must become very hot before it glows. A working LED usually needs much less electrical energy for a similar amount of useful light, though it can still become warm. This helps explain why modern torches often use LEDs. It does not remove the need for suitable connections or current limiting.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting choose-source

lesson.text: Choose the source and the light-producing component as a pair. In our first circuit, one small cell powers a lamp selected for that voltage. In the later LED circuit, two cells supply a red LED through a resistor. The second arrangement is not a general instruction to connect more cells whenever a light is dim. Identify the component and check its rating before deciding what change is justified.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting light-energy

lesson.text: Predict, connect and observe

lesson.figureCaption: Prepare the cell holder, lamp holder and insulated leads before joining the circuit.
paragraphs: Use one 1.5 V cell and an incandescent torch lamp rated for that supply. Ask your teacher to prepare short bare metal ends on the insulated wires.
1. Fit the cell according to the holder markings. Connect a wire to each holder terminal and to each of the lamp holder’s two separate terminals.
2. Before connecting, use the six arrangements on the next page to predict whether the lamp will glow. Record arrangement number, prediction and reason in your notebook.
3. With your teacher, test each arrangement briefly. Record the actual observation separately, then disconnect. Never make a wire-only path across the cell.
4. Compare the arrangements that give light with those that do not. If a result differs from your prediction, inspect the contacts and repeat it safely.

lesson.text: For these connection maps, P and N are the cell terminals; X and Y are the lamp holder’s separate terminals. The paired lines represent the cell; the circle and cross represent the lamp and its filament. Lines joining terminals represent wires. A loose end stops short of a terminal. These maps describe connections without showing a glowing result.

Keep your prediction even if the test disagrees with it. Beside the observation, sketch the actual connection you tested. Did a loose wire move? Did it touch metal or only insulation? A prediction is a reasoned expectation before testing; an observation is what you noticed during the test. Recording them separately makes a correction useful rather than hiding the change in your thinking.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting arrangement-intro

lesson.caption: Six arrangements for prediction and observation. Record your results in a notebook; no glow is pre-filled.

lesson.text: An **electrical circuit** includes a path through which current can flow. In arrangements 1 and 6, the two lamp terminals connect to opposite cell terminals, making a complete path through the filament. Reversing the two connections does not prevent a correctly rated incandescent lamp from glowing. In 2 and 3, a connection is missing. In 4 and 5, both lamp terminals go to the same cell terminal, so the cell does not drive current through the lamp.

**Electric current** is the flow of electric charge. By convention, its direction in the external circuit is from the cell’s positive terminal, through the components, towards its negative terminal. A complete loop, a working source and suitable components are all needed. The cell transfers energy to the lamp; current is not a substance that gets used up inside the filament.

paragraphs: A lamp stays dark. One group concludes, “The cell is used up.” Another says, “The wire touches the plastic instead of the metal.” What evidence would distinguish these explanations?
Plan a sequence that changes one thing at a time. Include a known working lamp, a known working cell and a contact check. Explain why replacing a cell could also improve a loose connection.

lesson.text: A lamp with a broken filament is often called fused. Its internal path is open even when the outside wires look correct. A dark lamp can also mean a depleted cell, loose or dirty contacts, the wrong lamp rating, or insulation trapped at a contact. A test result becomes more useful when you can rule out these alternatives.
Making an LED light

paragraphs: Your teacher supplies a red LED suitable for a 3 V circuit, two matching 1.5 V cells in a series holder, a 330 Ω resistor and insulated leads. The teacher checks the LED ratings first.
1. Keep the cells disconnected while building. Connect the holder’s positive lead to the resistor, the other resistor end to the LED anode, and the cathode to the holder’s negative lead.
2. Ask your teacher to check the connections. Connect briefly, observe the LED, record the result and disconnect.

3. Your teacher may reverse only the LED for a brief comparison if its reverse-voltage rating permits 3 V. Predict, observe and then disconnect. If that rating is unknown, discuss the comparison using the diagram instead.
4. Restore the approved forward connection. If no light appears, check polarity, contacts and component ratings; do not remove the resistor.

lesson.caption: Forward connection: the resistor is in the same loop as the LED. Disconnect before changing any component.

lesson.text: An LED normally conducts readily in its forward direction and emits light when enough current flows. Reversing it usually prevents light at this small supply voltage, but excessive reverse voltage can damage it. The **resistor** limits current and protects the LED. It may be on either side of the LED in this single loop. Correct polarity alone does not make a direct connection to a battery safe.
lesson.correction: Add current limiting and reverse-voltage qualification to the direct LED connection in the source.

lesson.text: A switch controls the path

lesson.figureCaption: A paper-clip switch with an open gap. The cardboard is its insulating base.
paragraphs: 1. Collect thick cardboard, two brass split-pin fasteners, a bare metal paper clip and two insulated wires. Your teacher makes the holes and secures the fasteners, covering any sharp ends underneath.
2. Trap one end of the clip under the first fastener so it can pivot. Place the second fastener where the clip can touch it when turned.
3. Attach one wire to each fastener. Check that the clip moves freely and can leave a visible gap. Build without a cell connected.

lesson.text: You have made a movable connection. Before using it, predict which position will allow a complete path. Inspect the metal contact: painted or plastic-coated clips may fail to conduct at their surfaces, even though there is metal underneath.

paragraphs: 1. Join the switch, a correctly rated incandescent lamp and one cell in a single loop. Start with the clip away from the second fastener. Observe and record.
2. Touch the clip to the second fastener. Observe briefly, record and open the switch again. Compare your observations with your prediction.
3. Disconnect the cell, move the switch to a different place in the same loop, and reconnect. Does its position change whether opening it interrupts the path?
4. Disconnect after the test. If the lamp does not respond, check the metal contacts before changing your explanation.

columns.title: Open circuit
items: Contact: an air gap separates conducting parts.
Path: the single loop is broken.
Observation: a working incandescent lamp stays dark.

columns.title: Closed circuit
items: Contact: the switch terminals are joined by metal.
Path: the loop is complete.
Observation: a suitable working lamp can glow if the source and other connections work.

lesson.text: A **switch** completes or breaks a conducting path; it is not the source of energy. In the single-loop circuit here, opening the switch anywhere interrupts current everywhere in that loop. Household switches also control paths, but their construction and installation must meet much greater safety demands. Never open or test a mains switch.

When the switch opens, the wires and lamp have not vanished. Their material is still conducting, but the air gap interrupts the route. Do not describe the open switch as “using up” the current. Equally, a closed switch does not force a defective lamp to work. Trace the whole loop and check the source before deciding which part explains the observation.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting switch-explain

lesson.text: 3.3  Reading Circuit Diagrams

A photograph shows what equipment looks like. A **circuit diagram** uses symbols to show how it is connected. The drawing need not match the physical positions of the parts. A long straight line can represent a bent wire; what matters is which terminals it joins.

Start at a marked supply terminal and follow each line to the next component. Continue through that component to the other supply terminal. If a line ends at an open switch, your trace has reached a gap. If you return by a wire that bypasses the lamp, you have found a different connection. Redrawing a wire with an extra bend does not fix either problem.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting diagram-intro

lesson.caption: Read across from component name to symbol. The added resistor symbol supports our current-limited LED circuit.

lesson.text: In the cell symbol, the longer line is positive and the shorter line negative. Repeated pairs represent a battery of cells. The circle with a cross represents a lamp. The LED symbol includes a diode and two small outward arrows for emitted light; these arrows are not extra wires. Its bar marks the cathode side. A resistor may be drawn as a rectangle; another convention uses a zigzag.

Shared symbol conventions help people communicate. Organisations including IEC, ANSI and IEEE publish standards used in electrical work. Some drawings use different accepted symbol styles, so read the key. A circuit diagram is a model of the connections, not a picture of every detail inside a device.

A diagram can be neat and still describe the wrong circuit. Check connections before judging appearance. Every component shown should have its intended terminals connected, and the supply must not have a wire-only route between its terminals. If two lines merely cross, do not assume a junction unless the drawing makes that connection clear. In our diagrams, separate routes are kept apart wherever possible.
lesson.addition: Focused explanation supporting standards

paragraphs: 1. Draw the circuit for your lamp, one cell and an open switch using the symbol key. Show a complete wire route, with the deliberate gap only at the switch.
2. Draw the forward LED circuit using two series cells, a resistor and an LED. Mark the supply polarity.
3. Exchange drawings. Trace each route from one supply terminal to the other through the components. Compare the drawing with the real setup while it is disconnected.
4. Compare your drawings with the examples below. Different wire shapes can describe the same connections.

lesson.caption: A lamp loop with an open switch, and a forward LED loop with current limiting. Neither diagram is a scale drawing.

lesson.addition: Transfer between a physical layout and a circuit model.
paragraphs: A wire looks much longer in one drawing than in another, but it still joins the same two terminals. Has the circuit connection changed? Explain what you would trace to decide.
Now imagine a second gap hidden under a loose connector. Would closing the switch alone make the lamp light? Explain why the switch position is not enough evidence that the whole loop is complete.

lesson.text: 3.4  Conductors and Insulators

Why do connecting wires have a metal core and a plastic covering? Use a working low-voltage circuit to compare materials. Begin by checking the tester itself. Otherwise a dark lamp could tell you about a faulty tester rather than the object you meant to test.

paragraphs: 1. Make a loop with one cell and a matching incandescent lamp, leaving two free wire ends as a test gap. Briefly touch those ends together. If the lamp does not glow, fix the tester before continuing. The lamp must remain in the loop.

2. Choose safe, clean, dry objects: a spoon, coin, key, foil, cork, rubber eraser, plastic ruler, wooden block, glass item, paper, cardboard, wax and graphite pencil lead. Let the teacher handle any pins or needles.
3. Place each object across the gap so the two wire ends touch separate points on it, not each other. Test briefly, record the material and whether the lamp glows, then disconnect.
4. Recheck the tester by touching its free ends together between doubtful results. Describe anything that may affect contact: a coating, dirt, moisture or a very small contact area.
5. Use the recording guide to propose a conclusion and its limits. Never test people, sockets, liquids or connected appliances.

lesson.caption: Choose objects with clearly identified materials. Test only safe, dry samples approved by the teacher.
Notebook recording guide: keep observations separate from conclusions
rows: Name the object and its tested surface.
A metal object may have an insulating coating.
Glow, no visible glow, or uncertain; note the contact.
Do not replace the observation with an expected answer.
Record the tester check and any repeat.
State what this test supports, and what it cannot settle.
lesson.note: Read across to plan each entry. Compare down your own records to look for patterns; this is guidance, not a table of measured results.

lesson.text: A **conductor** allows electric current to flow relatively easily. An **insulator** resists that flow strongly under the conditions considered. Metals such as copper and aluminium are useful conductors. Dry plastic, rubber, glass and ceramic commonly act as insulators. Graphite is a non-metal that conducts: being metallic is not the definition of a conductor.

No visible glow does not prove that absolutely no current passes. A material may pass too little current to light this lamp, or its contact may be poor. Graphite, for example, can give a weak result with a small lamp tester. State your conclusion as “did not light this lamp under these conditions” when the evidence is limited. A sensitive meter can investigate further under teacher supervision.

lesson.addition: Bound a negative observation with a functioning control.
paragraphs: A painted metal key does not light the tester, but a bare metal spoon does. One learner calls the key an insulator. What else could explain the observation?

Suggest a safe comparison using an already exposed metal part or an unpainted key; do not scrape coatings yourself. Explain what repeating the tester check before and after the comparison would establish.

columns.title: Conducting parts
items: Purpose: carry current where the circuit needs it.
Examples: metal cores of wires and metal contacts in switches.
Choice: silver, copper and gold conduct well; copper is usually the less costly choice.

columns.title: Insulating parts
items: Purpose: separate conducting parts and help prevent accidental contact.
Examples: plastic wire coverings and ceramic supports.
Limit: damaged, wet or unsuitable insulation may not protect you.

lesson.text: The human body can conduct electricity. Current through it can cause severe injury or death. Never touch plugs or switches with wet hands, use electrical equipment in wet areas, or handle damaged cords and plugs. Tell an adult about damage and keep away. Classroom low-voltage observations do not make it safe to investigate household supply.

A cell supplies direct current (DC): in a simple working circuit its direction stays the same. Household supply is alternating current (AC), whose direction reverses repeatedly. DC is not limited to small devices; electric vehicles also use large battery packs. Safety depends on the source and conditions, not merely on the labels AC and DC.
lesson.correction: Avoid defining DC as small-device electricity or implying all batteries are safe.

lesson.text: Portable power and responsible use

Cylindrical cells power many torches, clocks, remotes and toys. Button cells are used in some watches and hearing aids; rechargeable packs serve phones, laptops and electric vehicles. Their sizes, arrangements and charging requirements differ. Keep loose cells away from metal objects and small children. Never dismantle a cell or put it in a fire. Give used cells to an adult for an approved collection route.

opener: A torch lights a dark corner. What must happen inside it before its lamp can glow?

Nihal and his classmates are preparing for a visit to the Bhakra Nangal hydroelectric project. Falling water drives turbines connected to generators. Their assignment begins closer to home: find out how people use electricity.

In this chapter, use small cells, lamps and wires to investigate a complete path. Predict before connecting, record what happens, and use the evidence to explain a torch, a switch and a simple circuit.

projects.title: Two days without mains electricity
projects.text: Plan for a two-day power cut: consider light, water, communication, food storage and transport. Which activities could use stored energy or another method? Discuss preparation with an adult; never test generators.

projects.title: A small solar-powered fan
projects.text: With your teacher, connect a small educational solar panel to a matching low-voltage toy motor and soft propeller. Use the manufacturer’s instructions and secure the motor. Keep fingers, hair and clothing away from moving blades. Compare its behaviour in bright light and partial shade without changing the connections. Record light conditions as well as motion.
projects.caption: Prepare the matching panel and motor before connecting; use a stable mount and soft blades.

projects.title: Investigate cells in use
projects.text: With adult supervision, visit an electrical shop or study its catalogue. Record cell shapes, stated voltages, whether they are rechargeable, and suitable devices. Compare the information with manufacturer instructions. Do not handle loose button cells or buy and dismantle battery packs for this project.

projects.title: Both materials matter
projects.text: List safe household objects made mainly of conducting materials, mainly of insulating materials, or of both. Identify the purpose of each part in the mixed group. Observe externally; do not open plugs or appliances. Explain why “made of both” is often a useful design rather than a contradiction. A plastic handle and a metal working part can serve different purposes; identify each material before deciding what the whole object tells you.

summary: A cell has positive and negative terminals and supplies electrical energy. In a series battery, positive joins negative between neighbouring cells.
An incandescent lamp has a filament connected to two separate terminals. Heating of the filament produces light.
An LED has no filament. It normally emits light with a suitable forward connection and requires current limiting.
A complete path, a working source, good contacts and suitable components are needed for a lamp to glow.
Conventional current in the external circuit is taken from positive towards negative. Energy is transferred; current is not used up in a lamp.
A switch controls a path. Opening it anywhere in a single series loop interrupts current in the whole loop.
Circuit diagrams show connections using shared symbols. The longer cell-symbol line represents the positive terminal.
Conductors and insulators serve different purposes. A no-glow result is limited by the tester’s sensitivity and the quality of contact.
Predict before testing, record actual observations, use a working control and investigate one possible fault at a time.
Use only approved small cells in these activities. Never test mains electricity, people or damaged equipment; disconnect after testing.

exercises.text: Which metal is commonly used for inexpensive food-packaging foil that can fold readily? Choose aluminium, copper, iron or gold, and name the relevant property.
Which metal can react so vigorously with water that a fire may result: copper, aluminium, zinc or sodium? Explain why this is a knowledge question, not a test to try.

State whether each claim is true or false and explain. (a) Aluminium and copper are non-metals used in utensils and statues. (b) All metal oxides give solutions that turn blue litmus red. (c) Oxygen is a non-metal essential for human respiration. (d) Copper is used to boil water because it conducts electricity well.
Why are only some metals and alloys suitable for jewellery? Consider appearance, ease of shaping, corrosion, wear and contact with skin. Explain why lustre alone is not enough.

Unscramble the element names from these letter groups: PEPORC; OGDL; ENXYGO; TENGOINR; NECOHIRL. Then match them to: electrical wiring; exceptional malleability and ductility; human respiration; a plant nutrient supplied in fertilisers; water purification.
What products form when magnesium and sulfur react with oxygen? Compare their physical states and the litmus evidence after each product is mixed with water.

A teacher heats magnesium in air and mixes its cooled ash with water. Complete the missing names and colour changes in this flow chart in your notebook. Explain which observation supports the conclusion that the mixture is basic.
exercises.caption: Use separate clean portions for each litmus test. Supply the missing information in your notebook.

exercises.text: Choose a suitable pan-body material from iron, copper, sulfur, coal, plastic, wood and cardboard. Give reasons concerning heat transfer, stability and safe use. Would you choose the same material for the handle?

Three similar clean iron nails are covered separately by oil, ordinary water and vinegar and left for the same time. Which setup would you expect to limit rusting most? State your assumptions about complete oil coverage and access to air. Explain why vinegar can attack iron and why appearance alone may not measure all corrosion.
Give three uses of metals or non-metals. For each, connect the use with a property and identify one limitation or condition that matters.

Zinc coatings protect iron. Sulfur shows no obvious reaction with water in our test. Is that observation enough to recommend sulfur as a protective coating? Consider brittleness, adhesion, complete coverage and what happens if the layer is damaged.
Why does an ironsmith heat iron before shaping a tool? Explain how heating helps the metal deform. Does this mean every metal must be heated before it can be shaped?

glossary: The characteristic shine of a clean metal surface.
Ability to form sheets without breaking.
Ability to be drawn into wire.
Tendency to fracture instead of deforming substantially.
Ability to produce a ringing sound when struck.
Transfer of energy through a material from hotter to cooler regions.
Reaction of iron involving water and oxygen that forms rust.
Deterioration through reaction with the surroundings.
Substance not broken into simpler substances by chemical means.
