lesson.text: 9.1 Nutrition in Animals

**Life processes** are the activities that maintain living organisms. Nutrition supplies materials and energy sources; respiration releases usable energy; circulation transports substances; excretion removes metabolic wastes. Reproduction continues a kind of organism across generations, although an individual can survive without reproducing.

Observe familiar animals without disturbing or feeding them. They obtain food in different ways. What body parts help each animal reach, take in or break up its food? Separate something you actually observe from an explanation you infer.

items: **Bees and sunbirds:** take nectar from flowers using specialised mouthparts or a long tongue and beak.
**Young mammals:** obtain milk from their mothers. Humans, cows and many other mammals begin life this way.
**Pythons:** swallow prey whole, then digest it internally; swallowing whole does not mean skipping digestion.
**Filter-feeding aquatic animals:** collect small food particles carried in water. They do not obtain all their food by taking bites.

lesson.text: Food contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats and other nutrients. Many large food molecules cannot be absorbed as they are. **Digestion** breaks them into smaller substances that the body can absorb and use. Mechanical actions break food into pieces; digestive enzymes carry out chemical changes.

Taking food into the body is **ingestion**. After digestion, small nutrient molecules cross the intestinal wall during **absorption**. Cells then use absorbed materials for energy, growth and repair, called **assimilation**. Undigested remains eventually leave through the anus by **egestion**. These terms name different steps, not five names for digestion.
9.1.1 Digestion in Human Beings

The **alimentary canal** is the continuous passage from the mouth to the anus. Food travels along it; secretions enter from its lining and from associated organs. The liver and pancreas contribute digestive secretions, but food does not pass through these organs. Each region has a different job. We will follow the connected route and ask what changes as food moves onwards.

lesson.caption: The human digestive system, simplified. Follow the food path; the liver and pancreas send secretions into the small intestine.

lesson.text: The mouth: chewing and saliva

Teeth cut, crush and grind food into smaller pieces. The tongue mixes it with saliva and helps form a soft mouthful for swallowing. Saliva moistens food and contains the enzyme **amylase**, which starts breaking starch into smaller sugars. Remembering a favourite food can stimulate saliva even before the first bite.

If a teacher permits and the food is suitable for you, slowly chew a small bite of plain chapati or boiled rice for about 30–60 seconds. Use only your own food; do not share it or hold food in your mouth while speaking. Some people notice increasing sweetness. Record your own experience; no clear taste change is also a valid observation. Anyone who cannot take part can analyse the evidence instead.

Taste alone is a subjective clue. How could we test for the starch that is present before and after an enzyme acts? Iodine solution becomes blue-black in the presence of starch. It tests for starch, not directly for sugar. The following teacher-led comparison uses prepared amylase instead of collecting saliva or chewed food.

paragraphs: 1. A teacher labels two clean tubes A and B. Put equal portions of the same mashed boiled rice and equal measured amounts of water, about 3–4 mL, in each. Record the starting appearance.

2. The teacher adds a measured amount of school-approved amylase solution to B and the same volume of water to A. Use separate droppers. Keep the mixtures at the same teacher-approved temperature for the same time.
3. Add the same number of drops of dilute iodine, about 3–4, to each tube. Mix separately and compare colours under the same light. Record observations before explaining them.
4. Use the recording guide to organise your notebook. Repeat with fresh samples if the comparison is unclear.

Teacher demonstration only: wear eye protection, avoid skin and eye contact with iodine, and never taste treated food. Do not collect or share saliva. The teacher prepares and disposes of the solutions.
lesson.diagramCaption: Initial materials: both rice mixtures look alike. No test result is shown in the setup.

lesson.caption: Recording the starch comparison in your notebook
lesson.note: Read across to connect each sample with its evidence. Compare down to look for a difference; these are recording instructions, not sample results.

lesson.text: If A becomes blue-black, the starting rice contained detectable starch. If B gives a weaker or absent blue-black colour under comparable conditions, this supports the idea that amylase has broken down some starch. It does not prove that every starch molecule has disappeared or that the iodine test detected sugar.

If both mixtures remain dark, check the enzyme preparation, waiting time, temperature, quantities and mixing. If A does not respond, first check the starch and iodine using known samples. Record unexpected results honestly. Comparing unchewed and chewed rice changes particle size as well as adding saliva. The prepared-enzyme comparison controls that difference better.

paragraphs: A learner says, “Tube B is not blue-black, so I have proved that sugar formed.” What does the iodine test actually show? What further test would be needed for the second claim?
Two samples have different iodine colours, but one received twice as much water. Explain why the comparison is difficult to interpret. Which conditions should match in a repeat?
lesson.addition: Separates evidence for starch from a claim about sugar and identifies dilution as a confounder.

lesson.text: The food pipe: a moving wall

Swallowed food enters the **oesophagus**, or food pipe. Muscles in its wall contract behind the food and relax farther ahead. This travelling wave, called **peristalsis**, pushes the mouthful towards the stomach. Similar muscular movements move and mix contents along the digestive tract. Food does not simply drop through a passive pipe.

lesson.caption: Two successive positions of one mouthful. Contraction behind it and relaxation ahead help move it towards the stomach.

lesson.text: The stomach: mixing and chemical digestion
The stomach is a muscular pouch. Its walls churn food and mix it with gastric secretions. Different components of these secretions have different jobs; they should not all be called acid.

items: **Digestive enzymes:** begin the chemical breakdown of proteins into smaller components.
**Acid:** provides conditions in which stomach enzymes work and kills many swallowed microorganisms. It does not sterilise every meal.
**Mucus and other protective factors:** help protect the living stomach lining from its own digestive contents.

lesson.text: Churning and chemical changes produce a partly digested, semi-liquid mixture. It leaves the stomach gradually and enters the small intestine. Digestion is not completed in the stomach, and most nutrient absorption happens farther along.

In 1822, Alexis St. Martin survived an accidental gunshot wound that left an opening into his stomach. Physician William Beaumont used it to study gastric secretions and the digestion of different foods. These observations helped connect stomach movements and chemical action with digestion. This historical case also raises questions about consent and the treatment of research participants; it is not an experiment to imitate.
The small intestine: digesting and absorbing

The small intestine is narrow but long and tightly coiled. An adult’s may be around 6 m long, while the wider large intestine is about 1.5 m long; actual lengths vary with age and measurement method. The words small and large refer mainly to width, not length. Coiling lets a long digestive surface fit inside the abdomen.

items: **Liver:** makes bile, stored in the gallbladder. Bile disperses large fat globules into smaller droplets, giving enzymes more surface to work on. This physical dispersal is not the chemical digestion of fat.
**Pancreas:** supplies enzymes that act on carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Its bicarbonate-rich fluid helps neutralise the acidic mixture arriving from the stomach.
**Small-intestine lining:** supplies enzymes that help complete digestion, producing substances small enough to be absorbed.

lesson.text: This is a connection with your chapter on acids and bases. Conditions suitable for stomach enzymes are not suitable for every intestinal enzyme. Secretions change the chemical conditions as food moves onwards. Food enters the intestine; secretions reach it through small ducts.

The inner surface has many small finger-like projections called **villi**. Their thin covering and large combined surface bring digested nutrients close to transport vessels. Villi project into the space carrying digested food; they are not little teeth that chew it.

lesson.caption: An enlarged patch of intestinal lining. Villi increase the surface available for absorption; the colours distinguish tissues and vessels.

lesson.text: Many absorbed nutrients, including simple sugars and amino acids, enter small blood vessels. Most absorbed fats first enter lymph vessels before reaching the blood. Transport carries nutrients away, helping maintain absorption. Cells use these materials to release energy or to build and repair body tissues.

In **coeliac (celiac) disease**, gluten triggers an immune reaction that damages the small-intestine lining and can reduce nutrient absorption. Wheat, barley and rye contain gluten. A clinician diagnoses the condition and guides a gluten-free diet; do not diagnose it or remove foods on your own. Jowar, bajra and ragi are naturally gluten-free, but preparation and contamination also matter.
The large intestine: water and egestion

Material not absorbed in the small intestine moves into the large intestine, where more water and some salts are absorbed. Much water has already been absorbed in the small intestine. The remaining material forms stool, which is stored in the rectum and eventually passes out through the anus. **Egestion** removes undigested remains; **excretion** removes wastes produced by the body’s chemical processes.

Microorganisms in the large intestine use some material that our own enzymes cannot digest, including some dietary fibre. Their products can nourish intestinal cells and contribute certain vitamins. The gut contains a community of organisms; “all bacteria are harmful” is therefore a poor explanation of digestion.

A varied diet containing vegetables, fruits and whole grains supplies fibre. Water and regular activity also support normal bowel function. Fermented foods such as curd, buttermilk, kanji, gundruk or poita bhat differ in preparation and microbial content. Food hygiene, storage, salt and sugar matter; being fermented does not make every food a cure or suitable for everyone.

Care begins before food reaches the stomach: brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth as advised, and visit a dentist for routine care. Discuss elders’ oral-hygiene practices respectfully, then compare them with reliable dental guidance. Rinsing after meals does not replace brushing.

The Thirukkural and Charaka Samhita show a long-standing interest in eating and digestion; the latter discusses foods and spices such as ginger, pepper and cumin. Historical advice is part of cultural history, not a guarantee that a food or meal schedule prevents illness. Claims about treatment need appropriate evidence. Eat without rushing and seek qualified help for persistent problems.
9.1.2 Different Animals, Different Digestive Systems

A cow may chew while resting after grazing. Cows, buffaloes, goats and other **ruminants** swallow partly chewed food into a specialised stomach. Microbes in its large rumen help break down plant material. Some contents return to the mouth as cud for more chewing, then are swallowed again. This repeated chewing is **rumination**.

lesson.caption: A simplified cow cutaway. The large rumen supports microbial digestion; cud returns through the oesophagus for further chewing.

lesson.text: A bird has no teeth. In many birds, a muscular **gizzard** grinds swallowed food; small swallowed stones or grit may help. A glandular part of the stomach supplies digestive secretions. The form and strength of these parts vary with diet. Do not offer birds grit or unusual food as an experiment.

lesson.caption: A hen’s connected digestive passage: the crop stores food, the glandular stomach supplies secretions, and the gizzard grinds it.

columns.title: Ruminant
items: Mechanical action: chewing, returning cud and chewing again.
Distinctive part: a rumen with microbes that help process plant material.

columns.title: Bird
items: Mechanical action: grinding by a muscular gizzard.
Distinctive part: a strong gizzard; grit helps in many species.

lesson.text: These structures reflect inherited differences that developed over generations; animals did not choose to redesign their organs. Digestion supplies small nutrients, but cells must still release usable energy from them. That brings us to respiration.
9.2 Respiration in Animals

**Respiration** is the set of chemical processes in cells that releases usable energy from food molecules. In the aerobic respiration explored here, cells use oxygen. **Breathing** moves air into and out of lungs; **gas exchange** transfers oxygen and carbon dioxide across a surface. These are connected processes, but they happen in different places.
9.2.1 Respiration in Humans

Air normally enters through the nostrils and nasal passages. Hairs and mucus trap some particles; the passages also warm and moisten the air. It passes through the throat into the windpipe, or trachea, which divides into two main branches, one to each lung. Smaller branches end at tiny air sacs called **alveoli**.

lesson.caption: The human respiratory system, simplified. The ribs protect the lungs; the diaphragm forms a muscular floor beneath them.

lesson.text: Filtering is useful but incomplete: fine particles and infectious agents can still enter. SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, can affect the respiratory system. Sneezing can help expel an irritant from the nose. Never inhale dust deliberately to test this response. The nose conditions air, but mouth breathing can also occur, for example during vigorous activity.
Modelling how breathing works

Lungs have no muscles that pull air into themselves. What changes the space around them? Build a model that lets you change an enclosed volume and watch what happens to two balloons. Predict what an air leak might change before you begin.

paragraphs: 1. An adult cuts the base from a wide clear plastic bottle, covers the cut edge and makes a hole in its cap. Use a teacher-prepared Y-shaped hollow tube; attach one small balloon tightly to each branch.
2. Pass the straight tube through the cap. Seal around it with modelling clay, leaving the tube’s upper end open to air. Close the cap tightly so air cannot leak around the tube.
3. Stretch a thin rubber sheet over the open bottle base and secure its edge with a large band. Leave a small central tab to hold. Check all seals.
4. Gently pull the sheet down, then release it. Observe each balloon and record both changes. Repeat with the same gentle movement. Do not describe a result until you have observed it.
Adult cutting only. Check latex allergies and use a suitable alternative if necessary. Keep balloons away from mouths and discard broken pieces; do not blow through the model or share mouthpieces.
lesson.diagramCaption: Initial model at rest. The open tube connects the balloons to outside air; the bottle space around them must be sealed.

lesson.text: With good seals, pulling the sheet down increases the space around the balloons and lowers the air pressure there. Outside air enters through the tube and the balloons expand. Releasing the sheet reduces that space; the balloons recoil and air leaves. If one or both do not respond, inspect the seals and tube connections before rejecting the explanation.

lesson.caption: The diaphragm changes shape as the chest volume changes.

columns.title: Inhalation
items: Diaphragm contracts and moves down; ribs move up and out.
Chest volume increases; pressure inside the lungs falls below outside pressure.
Air enters and lungs expand.

columns.title: Quiet exhalation
items: Diaphragm and rib muscles relax; ribs return and diaphragm rises.
Elastic recoil reduces chest and lung volume.
Air leaves as pressure inside rises above outside pressure.

lesson.text: Balloons represent lungs; the sheet represents the diaphragm. The rigid bottle cannot show rib movement. A real diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle, not a sheet pulled by a hand, and lungs contain many tiny air spaces. A model explains a relationship without copying every feature.

paragraphs: A model’s balloons inflate when the bottom sheet is pulled. Does this show that the lungs contain muscles that suck in air? Use the route taken by air and the changing space around the balloons to explain.
Would a rigid bottle show the movement of the ribs? Name one thing this model explains and one thing it cannot represent.
lesson.addition: Makes the pressure mechanism and limitations of a lung model explicit.

lesson.text: What changes in exhaled air?

Lime water becomes cloudy when carbon dioxide forms fine particles of calcium carbonate in it. Both room air and exhaled air contain carbon dioxide. A fair comparison needs equal liquid amounts and comparable volumes of each gas; unlimited pumping into one tube would not be a fair test.

paragraphs: 1. Teacher demonstration: put equal measured volumes of fresh clear lime water in two matching tubes A and B, supported securely in a rack.

2. Use two separate equal-volume needle-free syringes. Fill one with room air. Fill the other from a clean collection bag containing a teacher’s exhaled air; use a fresh individual collection arrangement.
3. Through separate tubes, gently pass the same measured gas volume into each lime-water sample at a similar rate. Compare after each equal volume. Record cloudiness, volume passed and elapsed time.
4. Repeat with fresh lime water and new gas samples to check whether the pattern is consistent. Record what happened, even when a difference is unclear.

Wear eye protection. Lime water is alkaline: never suck or blow directly through a tube in it, and never mouth-pipette. Students handle no breath samples. Keep apparatus away from faces; the teacher disposes of it.
lesson.diagramCaption: The teacher transfers matched gas volumes with separate needle-free syringes. Both liquid samples are initially clear.

lesson.text: Earlier cloudiness with the same volume of exhaled air supports a higher carbon-dioxide concentration in that sample. Room air can also turn lime water cloudy if enough is passed through. No visible change after a small volume does not establish that carbon dioxide is absent. Prolonged bubbling can change the result again, so compare initial clouding using fresh samples.
Alveoli: where gases cross

Alveoli have thin walls and a large combined surface closely surrounded by blood capillaries. Oxygen passes from alveolar air into the blood by diffusion. Carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the air sacs and is breathed out. Neither gas needs a hole large enough for blood to leak into the lungs.

lesson.caption: An enlarged air sac beside a blood capillary. Arrows show opposite gas movements across thin walls; the air and blood remain in separate spaces.

lesson.text: Blood arriving from body tissues carries more carbon dioxide and less oxygen than blood leaving the lungs. It still contains some oxygen. Oxygen-rich blood travels back to the heart and is pumped to the body. The colours in the diagram distinguish blood with different oxygen levels; real human blood is never blue.

lesson.caption: Typical proportions in inhaled and exhaled air
lesson.note: These are approximate teaching values, not measurements from the lime-water test. Other gases make up most of the remainder; exhaled air also contains water vapour. Values vary with conditions.

lesson.text: Read across the oxygen row: exhaled air still contains substantial oxygen. Read across the carbon-dioxide row: its proportion is higher after passage through the body. We inhale a mixture called air, not pure oxygen, and we do not exhale pure carbon dioxide.
Respiration happens in cells

Glucose absorbed after digestion can react with oxygen through many controlled chemical steps in cells. Energy stored in food becomes available for movement, growth, repair and other cell activities; some is released as heat. The process is not a tiny flame inside the body.
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
lesson.caption: Aerobic respiration releases usable energy. The word equation summarises many reactions; energy is released, not a material made from nothing.

columns.title: Breathing
items: What happens: air moves into and out of the lungs.
Where: the respiratory air passages and lungs.
Role: renews air at gas-exchange surfaces.

columns.title: Cellular respiration
items: What happens: chemical reactions release usable energy from food.
Where: living cells throughout the body.
Role: powers cell functions; aerobic respiration uses oxygen.

lesson.text: The **circulatory system** contains the heart, blood and blood vessels. The heart pumps; blood transports oxygen and absorbed nutrients towards tissues and carries carbon dioxide and other wastes away. The lungs remove carbon dioxide; other organs handle other wastes. A blood vessel is a transport route, not a second food pipe.

paragraphs: Trace one glucose molecule from digested food and one oxygen molecule from inhaled air until they reach a body cell. Which surfaces must each cross, and which system carries them onwards?
A person breathes faster after running. Does this mean digestion is happening in the lungs? Explain how digestion, circulation and cellular respiration are connected without confusing their jobs.
lesson.addition: Integrates nutrient and gas transport without conflating organs or mechanisms.

lesson.text: Air, activity and respiratory health

During activity, working cells usually require more energy and produce more carbon dioxide. Breathing and circulation adjust to these demands. A breathing rate also depends on recent effort, recovery time, emotion and health. One measurement cannot rank classmates’ fitness or diagnose illness. Do not hold your breath or exercise to exhaustion for this lesson.

Tobacco smoke damages the respiratory system and increases the risk of serious disease, including lung cancer. **Second-hand smoke** is smoke breathed by people who are not smoking; it also harms health and can worsen breathing problems. Clean shared air matters, especially for children and people with respiratory conditions.

Breathing practices appear in yoga, chanting and other traditions. Some slow, comfortable breathing practices may help relaxation, but they are not substitutes for medical care. Claims that a particular practice cures disease or makes cold exposure safe need evidence. Learn about practices such as pranayama or Tummo through reading; do not attempt breath-holding, rapid-breathing or cold-exposure challenges.
9.2.2 Gas Exchange in Other Animals

Animals share the need to exchange gases, but the exchange surface differs. Mammals, birds and many reptiles have lungs. Bird lungs differ from mammal lungs, so a shared organ name does not imply identical internal structure or airflow. Living in water does not mean that every animal has gills.

lesson.caption: Different exchange surfaces: fish gills, an adult frog’s lungs and moist skin, and an earthworm’s moist skin. Drawings are not to the same scale.

items: **Fish:** water passes over thin gill surfaces supplied with blood vessels. Oxygen dissolved in water enters the blood; carbon dioxide leaves. Fish do not split water molecules to obtain oxygen.
**Frogs:** tadpoles usually exchange gases through gills and skin. Adults use lungs and their moist skin; skin gas exchange can occur both in water and on land.
**Earthworms:** gases cross moist skin into and out of blood. Drying damages this exchange surface, so observe worms in place without handling or exposing them to dry air.

lesson.text: These structures evolved over many generations in different environments. An individual frog developing from a tadpole is undergoing growth and development, not deciding to evolve a new breathing system. Digestion, gas exchange, circulation and other processes work together in living bodies; none operates entirely on its own.

opener: A bite of food and a breath of air take different routes through your body. Where do their journeys connect?
At lunch, you may be sitting still, yet your stomach is mixing food, your lungs are exchanging gases and your heart is pumping blood. Your body keeps working between meals and while you sleep.

In Class 6, you explored the characteristics of living things. Now follow nutrition and respiration inside animals: how food becomes usable nutrients, how oxygen reaches cells, and how different organs work together to sustain life.

projects.title: Evaluate a breathing-practice claim
projects.text: Research box breathing: inhalation, pause, exhalation, pause. Evaluate evidence for relaxation claims and identify uncertainties. This is reading, not a breath-holding exercise or treatment. Avoid forced breathing and discuss health questions with a qualified adult.

projects.title: How do high-flying birds obtain oxygen?
projects.text: Compare bird and mammal respiratory diagrams. Research air sacs and one-way lung airflow. Explain why high altitude means lower oxygen pressure, not usually a lower oxygen percentage. Air sacs move air; lung tissue exchanges gases. Name your sources.

summary: Life processes maintain organisms. Reproduction continues populations across generations.
Food follows the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus. Liver and pancreas supply secretions.
Chewing is mechanical breakdown; enzymes chemically digest food. Salivary amylase begins starch digestion.
Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine. Villi provide a large, thin exchange surface; nutrients support energy release, growth and repair.
The large intestine absorbs more water and salts. Rectum stores stool; egestion removes it through the anus.
Ruminants return cud for chewing; many birds grind food in a gizzard. Digestive structures vary with feeding habits.
Inhalation and exhalation renew air in the lungs. Changes in chest volume and pressure move air.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross between alveolar air and blood through thin walls. Exhaled air still contains oxygen.
Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water while releasing usable energy.
Breathing moves air; respiration is chemical change in cells. The heart and blood vessels connect gas exchange, absorbed nutrients and body tissues.
Other animals use lungs, gills or moist skin. These exchange surfaces have structures suited to their environments.
A useful investigation compares matched conditions, records actual evidence and recognises what a test or model cannot establish.

exercises.text: In your notebook, compare photosynthesis and aerobic respiration under four matching headings: raw materials, products, word equation and importance. State the role of light in each and show energy separately from material substances.

Imagine that all organisms carrying out photosynthesis disappeared. Explain likely effects on food supplies, food chains and oxygen over time. Would every stored food supply and all atmospheric oxygen disappear immediately? Give reasons.

A potato slice turns blue-black with iodine. Explain where the carbohydrate was made, how soluble food reached the potato and why finding starch in the tuber does not prove that it photosynthesised underground.
How can a broad, flat leaf help photosynthesis? Give a reason involving light and another involving gas exchange. Explain why leaves in dry environments may have different structures.
Identify X, Y and Z in this summary of aerobic respiration: X + Y → carbon dioxide + Z, with usable energy released. Explain why plants need this process even when they can make their own food.

Krishna grows comparable watered plants in light and darkness. The illustration gives a possible later appearance. (i) What idea could she be testing? (ii) Compare visible traits. (iii) Predict the starch-test results, stating why stored starch and treatment time matter.
exercises.caption: Illustrative comparison: left, light; right, darkness. Appearance is given evidence here, not a required outcome of every class experiment.

exercises.text: Vani starts with comparable destarched, watered plants in four conditions shown below. Assume temperature is suitable and the stated conditions persist. (i) Where would you predict detectable new starch? (ii) Where would you predict little or none? (iii) Where would photosynthesis generate oxygen? (iv) Where would it not? Explain why oxygen collection and production need not be equal.
exercises.caption: A: light with CO₂. B: light with CO₂ removed. C: darkness with CO₂. D: darkness with CO₂ removed. Compare A with B to test the role of carbon dioxide.

exercises.text: Ananya considers four tubes three-quarters full of water and the same carbon-dioxide indicator: A with a snail, B with a water plant, C with both, D with neither. She compares colours after 2–3 hours. What might she be investigating, and why is D needed? State the light conditions, indicator colour key and other controls needed before predicting results. Use supplied records or a simulation; do not confine animals in classroom tubes.
exercises.caption: The initial liquids have the same colour. No later colours are supplied; specify the missing information before drawing conclusions.

exercises.text: Design a coloured-water investigation comparing water transport in warm and cool conditions. Specify safe temperatures, matching stems and solutions, what you will measure and repeats. How would changes in humidity, leaf area or airflow complicate the comparison? Do not boil, freeze or heat plants directly.

Explain how photosynthesis and respiration connect food, oxygen and carbon dioxide in nature. Why is “balance” not a claim that every plant always produces exactly as much oxygen as it uses? Include growth and storage in your answer.

lesson.text: 10.1 How Do Plants Grow?

Plants grow new leaves and branches, thicken their stems and increase in height. Their cells need building materials and energy. Height alone is not a measure of health: a shoot stretched towards light may be taller without becoming sturdy.

Does a plant take ready-made food from soil or make food from surrounding substances? Predict how water and light affect growth, and what evidence would challenge your ideas. Change one condition at a time.

paragraphs: 1. Plant similar healthy chilli or tomato seedlings in three matching pots with equal amounts of the same soil. Label A, B and C. Record starting height, leaf number and colour.
2. Keep A in suitable sunlight with moist soil. Keep B in the same light without watering. Keep C in darkness, with soil moisture similar to A. Match temperature and other conditions.
3. Observe at the same time daily for up to two weeks. Measure height from soil level and count leaves consistently. Record actual changes beside your predictions.
4. Stop a treatment if sustained wilting or deterioration occurs; restore suitable light and water and record the date. Do not continue until the plant dies.
Use pots with drainage; an adult cuts reused bottles. Avoid waterlogging and overheated boxes. Never taste soil; wash hands afterwards.
lesson.diagramCaption: Starting plants are comparable. The labels specify treatments; they do not predict the outcome.

lesson.caption: Record the same measures for each pot
rows: Record A, B and C conditions
lesson.note: Make one copy per pot in your notebook. These are recording instructions, not results. Compare each plant with its own starting record before comparing pots.

lesson.text: Compare A with B to investigate water availability, and A with C to investigate light. B and C differ in both water and light, so that pair cannot isolate either factor. Suitable light and adequate water usually support continued growth. A plant without water may wilt; one in darkness may become pale and elongated while using stored food. Neither response is guaranteed within a fixed number of days.

One seedling per treatment gives limited evidence. Seedlings differ naturally, and a dark cupboard may also be warmer or cooler. Repeat with several matched plants if practical. This comparison does not establish which substance becomes new plant material or show that plants take food from soil.

paragraphs: The dark-grown plant is tallest, but has a thin stem and pale leaves. Is height alone a sound measure of healthy growth? Use at least two other observations in your answer.
A class compares only a watered plant in sunlight with an unwatered plant in darkness. Explain why it cannot tell which difference caused the result. Design a clearer comparison.
lesson.addition: Distinguishes elongation from healthy growth and isolates experimental variables.

lesson.text: The historical text Vrikshayurveda records observations about plants, soil, crop care and manure preparation, including mixtures involving water, barley and pulse seeds. It recognises that planting alone does not ensure flowers and fruit. Such records are part of agricultural history; a particular treatment still needs a fair comparison before we assume that it works in every soil or climate.
10.2 How Do Plants Obtain Food?

Most green plants make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. Roots supply water and mineral nutrients, but minerals are not the plant’s ready-made carbohydrate food. Much of the carbon in new plant material comes from carbon dioxide in air. Animals depend on photosynthetic producers directly or through food chains.
10.2.1 Leaves and the Starch Test

Many leaves are broad and thin, exposing a large surface to light while keeping internal cells near air spaces and veins. Green tissues contain **chlorophyll**, a pigment that absorbs light used in making food. Leaf shapes vary with habitat; broad leaves are not the only workable design. Some sugars made by a plant are converted into **starch** for storage.

Recall the iodine test from the animal-nutrition chapter. A blue-black colour provides evidence of detectable starch. To see the reaction in a leaf, a teacher first removes much of its green pigment. Testing one leaf for starch does not by itself reveal when, where or under which conditions that starch formed.

A leaf test is destructive: the same leaf cannot be tested again after a day in light. Comparisons therefore use similar leaves of the same age, from matching plants. Label samples before treatment so they cannot be confused. When comparing patches, use a sketch to preserve their positions. Choose leaves large enough to handle safely, but do not assume that the largest leaf contains the most starch. A photograph or drawing records appearance; iodine supplies a different kind of evidence.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

paragraphs: 1. Teacher demonstration: soften a suitable leaf briefly in hot water using forceps. Place it in an open boiling tube containing enough ethanol to cover it.
2. Stand the tube in a stable hot-water bath supplied by a kettle or approved electric bath. Wait for much of the pigment to leave. Never heat ethanol directly.
3. With forceps, rinse the leaf in water to soften it. Spread it on a white tile, cover with dilute iodine and observe for a few minutes.
4. Sketch the colour pattern before interpreting it. If unclear, check the iodine against a known starch sample.
Teacher handles hot liquids, ethanol, iodine and chemical waste; wear eye protection. Ethanol is highly flammable: keep all flames and ignition sources away. Never taste treated leaves.
lesson.diagramCaption: A flame-free hot-water bath and a separate leaf-testing tile. The pale leaf has not yet been tested with iodine.

lesson.text: Blue-black areas contain starch detectable by this test. An area that remains yellow-brown may contain little or no detectable starch; that is not a measurement of every carbohydrate present. Removing chlorophyll makes the iodine colour easier to distinguish. The treatment prepares a specimen for testing; it is not how a living leaf normally changes colour.

Bhaskar notices leaves with green and cream patches. Such **variegated** leaves offer a comparison within one leaf. He also asks whether light is needed for starch accumulation. Map the patches before removing pigment: testing destroys the original colour guide.
lesson.heading: Comparing patches and light
lesson.caption: Green and cream patches on one leaf.

paragraphs: 1. Keep two similar watered variegated plants in darkness for about 36–48 hours. A teacher tests a spare leaf: stored starch must fall below detection. Time alone does not guarantee this.
2. Put one plant in suitable light for several hours; keep the other dark. Match temperature, water and exposure time; prevent overheating.
3. Sketch a comparable leaf from each plant. Mark its green and cream patches and light condition before the teacher carries out the same starch test on both.
4. Match each iodine pattern to its original patch map. Record unclear colours too. Restore both plants to suitable growing conditions.

lesson.caption: Bhaskar’s reported observations: evidence to interpret
lesson.note: These are supplied observations, not a pattern you must obtain. Read across one area, then compare the same area across light conditions. Record your own evidence separately.

lesson.text: The reported pattern supports a role for both light and chlorophyll in starch accumulation. A cream patch may contain too little chlorophyll to produce detectable starch under these conditions. The test does not prove an absolute absence of chlorophyll. Starch already present before treatment, imported sugars or an unsuccessful test can complicate an explanation.

Red, violet and brown leaves may still contain chlorophyll hidden by other pigments. Their colour alone cannot tell us whether they photosynthesise. Some accessory pigments absorb light used in photosynthesis; others have different roles. A controlled starch investigation is more informative than calling every non-green leaf unable to make food.

Read Bhaskar’s table in two directions. Within the lit leaf, compare green and cream patches: light is shared while pigment differs. Then compare green patches from the lit and dark plants: their colour is similar while light differs. Agreement between these comparisons strengthens an explanation involving both factors. It does not make either comparison perfect. Patches may differ in other tissues, and two plants are not identical. Repeating with more leaves helps show whether the pattern persists.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

lesson.text: 10.2.2 What Does Air Contribute?

Carbon dioxide is a small part of air. To investigate its role, compare leaves that receive similar light, water and temperature but have different carbon-dioxide availability. **Destarching** means reducing stored starch before a test, usually by keeping the plant in darkness while it continues to use its reserves.

paragraphs: 1. Teacher demonstration: prepare two comparable watered plants with starch reduced below detection. Enclose each under an identical transparent bell jar on a plate.
2. Place a stable dish of teacher-prepared sodium hydroxide solution in A, away from plant and soil. Put an equal dish of water in B. Seal both jars to their plates.
3. Give both the same few hours of suitable light. Match plant kind, leaf age, water and temperature; prevent overheating. Sodium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide.
4. Test comparable leaves using the same starch procedure. Record iodine colours before interpreting the evidence.
Sodium hydroxide is corrosive. Only the teacher handles solutions, jars, hot water, ethanol, iodine and disposal, using eye protection and suitable gloves.
lesson.diagramCaption: Two sealed enclosures control for the jar itself. A contains a carbon-dioxide absorber; B contains water.

lesson.caption: Record conditions before interpreting the starch test
lesson.note: Expected conditions are not measured starch results. Check seals and plant health. Compare down to distinguish the changed condition from the conditions intended to match.

lesson.text: If the control leaf becomes blue-black but the absorber leaf does not, the contrast supports the requirement for carbon dioxide in starch formation. If neither responds, insufficient light, incomplete testing or plant stress may be responsible. If both respond, consider residual starch or leaking seals. A chemical absorber may also change humidity, so repeat and interpret cautiously.

A related arrangement places half of one attached leaf inside a sealed bottle above sodium hydroxide and leaves the other half outside. It compares the two halves after testing. The inside half must not touch the solution. However, bottle shade, humidity and sealing can also differ between halves; a matched enclosure comparison helps examine these alternatives.

Why place a dish in the control jar at all? Both plants should experience an enclosure and similar equipment. Otherwise a result could arise from the jar rather than the absorber. A fair comparison also needs a working positive response: starch in the control leaf shows that the plant and test could produce the expected signal under those conditions. An absorber leaf alone cannot provide that check. A negative result is useful only when we know what the method was capable of detecting.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

lesson.text: Does a Lit Plant Release a Gas?

Leaves use materials from their surroundings, but they also release substances. An aquatic plant lets us collect some of the gas that leaves it. Seeing bubbles is evidence that a gas is escaping, not enough to name the gas or measure its purity.

paragraphs: 1. Place equal amounts of suitable pondweed under inverted funnels in two beakers. Use equal volumes of the same water.
2. Fill two tubes completely with water. Invert one over each funnel stem, keeping its opening submerged without trapped air. Label A and B.
3. Keep A lit and B dark for the same time at similar temperatures. Record whether gas collects; compare volumes over equal intervals.
4. If enough gas collects, the teacher uses an approved glowing-splint test away from ethanol and other flammables. Learners observe and record without handling fire.
Use school-approved pondweed and handle glass safely. Wash hands; never release laboratory pondweed into waterways. If too little gas collects, report that limit rather than inventing a result.
lesson.diagramCaption: One initial setup, before gas collects. Prepare a matching second setup; both tubes begin completely filled with water.

lesson.text: A glowing splint relighting in the collected gas supports the presence of oxygen-rich gas. Bubbles alone would not establish this. A lit plant may collect more gas than a dark one because photosynthesis produces oxygen, while respiration continues in both. Some oxygen remains dissolved in water or is used by the plant, so collected volume is not its entire production.

paragraphs: A learner sees no bubbles and concludes, “This plant cannot photosynthesise.” Give two reasons the apparatus might show no collected gas even when some photosynthesis occurs.
Another learner calls every bubble oxygen. Which extra observation strengthens that claim? Explain why a positive gas test still does not establish that the sample is pure oxygen.
lesson.addition: Separates gas collection, gas identity and net production.

lesson.text: 10.2.3 Photosynthesis: Connecting the Evidence

**Photosynthesis** is the process by which green plants use light energy to make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Chlorophyll helps capture the light. Leaves are major sites, but other green parts such as young stems can also photosynthesise. The investigations test parts of this account; no single one demonstrates the whole process.
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
lesson.caption: Light supplies energy; chlorophyll helps absorb it. They are conditions for this simplified equation, not extra material ingredients.

lesson.text: Separate matter from energy as you read the equation. Carbon dioxide and water supply atoms that are rearranged into new substances. Light supplies energy for this process; it is not a substance that roots absorb or a material stored unchanged inside a potato. Some captured energy becomes stored in chemical form. Later, respiration makes part of that energy available for cell activities. The arrow summarises many reactions inside cells, not a single visible mixing step.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

lesson.caption: Carbon dioxide enters green tissues; roots supply water. Light energy supports food production. The arrows summarise different routes, not hollow pipes through every leaf.

lesson.text: Glucose is a simple carbohydrate. Plants use sugars in respiration and in building other substances, including cellulose in cell walls. They convert some carbohydrate to starch for storage in leaves, roots, stems or seeds. A potato stores starch in an underground stem called a tuber; it does not need to receive sunlight underground to obtain carbohydrate.

A root can grow in darkness because it receives sugars from elsewhere in the plant. These sugars provide both building material and fuel for respiration. The root also needs mineral nutrients and a supply of oxygen. Thus a well-lit shoot cannot solve every root problem: severely waterlogged soil can limit oxygen reaching root cells. Making food, transporting it and using it are linked processes, but success in one does not guarantee that the others work normally.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

lesson.text: Rustom Hormusji Dastur (1896–1961) was an Indian plant scientist who investigated photosynthesis, including the influence of water, temperature and light. He led botany at the Royal Institute of Science in Bombay during 1921–1935. His work illustrates why a plant’s response must be studied under stated conditions rather than explained by light alone.
10.2.4 How Do Leaves Exchange Gases?

A leaf looks continuous to the unaided eye. A microscope reveals structures too small to see directly. Examine its surface before explaining how gases enter and leave. Use a teacher-selected leaf that gives a thin, clear peel; not every species is equally suitable.

A microscope enlarges a very small field, not the entire leaf. Examine several fields before describing what is common. Thick or folded tissue may hide pores, while a tear can resemble an opening. A good drawing selects clearly observed structures and records magnification; it does not copy every detail of an ideal diagram. If the preparation is unclear, improve it or examine a prepared slide before concluding that the leaf has no stomata.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

paragraphs: 1. Teacher demonstration: use forceps to peel a thin piece from the lower surface of a fresh Tradescantia (rhoeo) leaf. Keep it in a watch glass of water.
2. Lay a flat piece in water on a clean slide. Add school-approved stain if needed; lower a coverslip at an angle to reduce trapped air.
3. Start at low microscope power, increasing as directed. Sketch cells and pores; record magnification. Distinguish repeated structures from tears or air bubbles.
Handle glass carefully. No learner handles a blade; use prepared slides if necessary. Keep stains away from skin and eyes; wash hands afterwards.

lesson.caption: An enlarged interpretive drawing of leaf epidermis. A stoma is a pore bordered by guard cells; the drawing is not a measured micrograph.

lesson.text: The pores are **stomata**; one pore is a **stoma**. Guard cells border each pore and regulate its opening. Gases diffuse between the air and internal leaf spaces. Stomata also allow water vapour to escape. Their distribution differs among plants; many land plants have more on the lower surface, but that is not a rule for every leaf.

Opening stomata can help carbon dioxide enter, but also increases water loss. Closing them conserves water while limiting gas exchange. A leaf does not simply keep every pore fully open all day. Living cells continue to respire even when the pattern of exchange with outside air changes.
10.3 Transport in Plants
Roots take up water and dissolved mineral nutrients. These must reach leaves, developing shoots and other tissues.
10.3.1 Water and Mineral Transport

Unlike an animal’s heart-driven circulation, plant transport uses different structures and mechanisms. A coloured-water comparison can help locate the route taken by water without making the dye itself a nutrient. A cut stem removes roots from the setup: it traces movement through a shoot, but does not test water absorption by roots.

paragraphs: 1. Fill matching tumblers A and B one-third full with equal water volumes. Add school-approved red food dye to B; leave A colourless.
2. Choose two similar fresh white-flowered carnation or balsam stems. An adult cuts their bases obliquely under water and promptly puts one in each tumbler.
3. Match stem length, leaf area, temperature, light and time. Record starting colours. Next day, describe any coloured regions in stems, leaves or petals.
4. The teacher cuts thin cross-sections above the waterline. Use a hand lens to compare them. Sketch the colour distribution; do not assume the whole stem stains.
Adult cutting only. Do not eat flowers or drink dye solutions. Avoid unknown or irritating plant sap; wash hands afterwards.
lesson.diagramCaption: Both flowers begin white. A contains plain water; B contains dyed water. No transported dye is shown in the initial plants.

lesson.text: Coloured regions above the liquid level support upward movement of water containing the dye. Colour may be easier to see in pale petals or a cut stem than in green leaves. No obvious petal colour does not prove that water failed to move: species, dye, exposure time and the cut ends affect the result.

lesson.caption: Illustrative stem tissue after a dye test and an enlarged vascular bundle. Stained water-conducting regions are distinct from the food-conducting tissue; positions vary with plant type.

lesson.text: **Xylem** contains conducting tubes that carry water and dissolved minerals, mainly from roots towards shoots. Evaporation from moist leaf surfaces and loss of water vapour through stomata, called **transpiration**, help draw water upwards through connected columns. Roots supply water to replace what is lost. Plants do not have a hidden pump equivalent to a heart.
10.3.2 Food Transport

**Phloem** carries dissolved sugars from regions supplying them to regions using or storing them. A mature leaf may supply a growing root, fruit or shoot tip. Flow can therefore be upwards or downwards in different conducting paths; it is not always a one-way journey down from leaves. Starch is converted into soluble substances before stored carbohydrate is transported.

columns.title: Xylem
items: Cargo: water and dissolved mineral nutrients.
Usual direction: roots towards stems and leaves.
Connection: replaces water used or lost from shoots.

columns.title: Phloem
items: Cargo: dissolved sugars and other organic substances.
Direction: from a supplying region to a using or storing region.
Connection: feeds roots, developing shoots, fruits and seeds.

lesson.text: 10.4 Do Plants Respire?

A germinating seed can grow before it has green leaves. Its living cells use stored food, releasing usable energy through **respiration**. To look for a product of this process, compare air around germinating seeds with air in a matched control. Darkness prevents photosynthesis from removing carbon dioxide during the comparison.

paragraphs: 1. Teacher demonstration: germinate overnight-soaked moong beans on moist cotton. Put a small measured sample on damp cotton in flask A. In matching B, use the same cotton and an equal volume of clean glass beads.
2. Keep both dark for a short teacher-selected interval, with plenty of air space. Do not flood the cotton or use mouldy seeds.
3. Fit two-hole stoppers. With separate needle-free syringes, gently draw equal small volumes of headspace air. Briefly open each second tube to admit replacement air; do not draw liquid.
4. Pass equal gas volumes into equal fresh lime-water samples in separate open tubes. Compare initial and final cloudiness; repeat. Record contents, time, volume and observation.
Teacher handles glass and alkaline lime water with eye protection. Never suck or blow through reagents or taste seeds. Vent flasks afterwards; avoid prolonged airtight storage.
lesson.diagramCaption: Seeds and a matched moist-cotton control. The syringe transfers gas to separate lime-water tubes; it never passes through a seed or contains a needle.

lesson.text: If the seed flask gives earlier clouding for the same gas volume, the comparison supports additional carbon-dioxide production associated with the germinating seeds. Room air already contains some carbon dioxide, so the control is essential. Microorganisms can also respire; clean, fresh samples reduce that competing explanation. A CO₂ sensor can provide an alternative measurement.

Merely connecting a seed flask to lime water does not ensure that enough gas passes through it to show a change. A test needs a defined gas-transfer step and an open outlet; never pressurise a sealed reagent tube. The comparison detects a product of respiration, not every step of the cellular process.
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
lesson.caption: Aerobic respiration releases usable energy and heat. Energy is released from food, not created as an extra material product.

lesson.text: Living cells in roots, stems, leaves, flowers and germinating seeds respire in light and darkness. Green cells can photosynthesise when conditions permit, and respire at the same time. Saying “plants photosynthesise by day and respire only at night” confuses two processes. Some mature conducting cells are no longer living, so not every cell in a plant respires.

columns.title: Photosynthesis
items: Main role: stores light energy in carbohydrates.
Materials: carbon dioxide and water; oxygen is released.
Where and when: photosynthetic tissues with suitable light and conditions.

columns.title: Aerobic respiration
items: Main role: releases usable energy from food.
Materials: glucose and oxygen; carbon dioxide and water form.
Where and when: living cells, in both light and darkness.

lesson.text: Imagine a short interval in which photosynthesis removes six equal units of carbon dioxide from a leaf’s surroundings and respiration adds two. The surroundings show a net loss of four units, although both processes occurred. These invented numbers illustrate the accounting; they are not measured rates or a fixed ratio. In darkness, photosynthesis stops while respiration continues, so the direction of net carbon-dioxide exchange can change. A measurement of the net effect alone cannot reveal each separate rate.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

paragraphs: In bright light, a plant may take in more carbon dioxide than it releases. Does this mean its cells have stopped respiring? Explain the difference between two simultaneous processes and their net effect.
At night, a seedling continues growing although it cannot photosynthesise. Trace the stored food and oxygen it uses. Why would keeping its roots waterlogged make the situation different?
lesson.addition: Connects stored food, simultaneous processes and oxygen supply to roots.

lesson.text: Kamala Sohonie (1911–1998) studied plant respiration during her doctoral work at Cambridge. Her research on cytochrome c helped connect energy-releasing processes across organisms. After returning to India, she worked in medical and nutrition research and later led the Institute of Science in Bombay. Her studies of plant foods and the palm sap drink neera linked biochemical research with nutrition.

Think across a whole day, not just one moment. During a favourable light period, a plant may make more carbohydrate than it immediately uses. Some is transported to growing or storage tissues. During darkness, stored carbohydrate helps support continuing respiration and growth. Over longer periods, disease, limited water or poor light can reduce the amount available. This is why a plant’s condition depends on a changing supply and demand for materials, rather than on a simple switch between making food and using it.
lesson.addition: Mechanism and evidence enrichment

lesson.text: Photosynthesis supplies organic matter and contributes oxygen to ecosystems. Respiration uses food to power living cells and returns carbon dioxide and water. Transport connects these processes within a plant. Their rates do not have to match at every moment: growing plants can store material, and light, water, temperature and other conditions keep changing.

opener: A tiny seedling can become a tree. Where does the material for its new leaves, branches and trunk come from?
You have seen animals eat and followed the journeys of food and air through their bodies. A plant has no mouth or stomach, yet it grows, transports substances and releases energy in living cells.
Follow a plant from its roots to its leaves. Test ideas about water, light and air, then connect the evidence with how plants make, move and use food.

projects.title: Observe a bottle garden
projects.text: With an adult, plant a small humidity-loving plant, such as fittonia or a suitable fern, in a wide transparent jar. Use moist, not waterlogged, compost and bright indirect light. After establishment, fit a lid and record growth and condensation. Open it if overheating, decay or excess moisture develops. Do not use a closed sunny jar for jade or other dry-loving succulents. Survival alone does not measure the separate rates of photosynthesis and respiration.
projects.caption: A bottle garden exchanges energy with its surroundings. Water and gases can be recycled inside, but conditions still need monitoring.

projects.title: Connect plant processes with crops
projects.text: Choose one local crop. Explain how light capture, respiration and the transport of water, minerals and sugars support its growth and harvestable parts. Investigate one limiting condition, such as dry soil or excessive heat, using reliable agricultural sources. Distinguish evidence from a product’s advertising claim.

projects.title: Investigate a greenhouse
projects.text: Visit a greenhouse with a responsible adult, or interview a grower. Find out how light, water, temperature, ventilation and sometimes carbon dioxide are managed. Compare these conditions with outdoor growing. Do not handle heaters, gas equipment, pesticides or fertiliser solutions; present your observations and questions in a report.

summary: Plant growth depends on materials and energy. Height, leaf number, colour and sturdiness reveal different aspects of growth.
Most green plants make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. Roots take up water and minerals, not ready-made carbohydrate food.
Chlorophyll helps capture light. Leaves are major photosynthetic organs; other green parts can also photosynthesise.
Glucose can be used in respiration, converted into building materials or stored as starch. An iodine test detects starch, not every kind of food.
Experiments on light, green patches and carbon dioxide need matched conditions, starting checks and observations recorded before conclusions.
Photosynthesis releases oxygen. Bubbles alone do not identify a gas; a gas test provides additional evidence.
Stomata allow gas exchange and water-vapour loss. Guard cells regulate the pore opening.
Xylem carries water and minerals, mainly from roots to shoots. Phloem transports dissolved sugars from supplying to using or storing regions.
Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water while releasing usable energy.
Living plant cells respire in light and darkness. Photosynthesis and respiration can occur together, so observed gas exchange is their net effect.
